#### Transition Job State

##### Transition Job State Metadata
Several metadata tables are involved in defining metadata for Transition Job State. 
  * G3E_JOBDEFINITION—Set the [G3E_JOBDEFINITION.G3E_JOBSTATEFIELD](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/TBQDr_BsRYh8ej2Rr97t2g) to the name of the field in your job table that holds the state for each job. 
  * G3E_WORKMGMT
    * Populate a row in [G3E_WORKMGMT](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/KME_1L76HZEDZ5lzihAbeQ) with G3E_TYPE='LifeCycle'. This entry defines the table and an optimized table containing the definitions of each possible job state. Populate that table with the definitions of your job states. 
    * Populate a row in G3E_WORKMGMT with G3E_TYPE= 'Transitions' that specifies the table and an optimized table containing the allowed job state transitions. Populate that table with the set of allowed transitions. 
    * Populate a row in G3E_WORKMGMT with G3E_TYPE='Feature'. This record's G3E_SUPPORTCNO field specifies the component number of the common component where the job state is stored for each feature, and the G3E_SUPPORTANO field specifies the attribute number where the feature's job state is stored. 
    * Populate a row in G3E_WORKMGMT with G3E_TYPE='JobIdentifier' that identifies the attribute number where the feature's job identifier is stored. This attribute must be stored in a common component of all features whose job state is translated.

#### View Pairs Overview
The [View Pairs](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/yHEXWIqk5fAwWIMV~3bevA) command provides assignment information for a specified pair-count-bearing feature in a specified area. The data are retrieved from an external customer assignment database through a custom assignment interface object. 
The data are then passed to the report interface for formatting and presentation to the user. The HTML interface is used because of its ability to include script code in the stylesheet to perform post processing operations and to let you customize reports. 
The following is a sample output report from View Pairs: 
![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/api/khub/maps/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/resources/O~niKe7nnWP7yyvh4P~lNA-_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/content?v=64d5631a15308b60&Ft-Calling-App=ft/turnkey-portal)
  * To configure view pairs metadata:


  1. In the [Metadata Explorer](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/UTqIHC3d83TOn0KP~nqHeg) tree view, select the Communications Applications > Parameters > Customer Assignment Interface node. 
    1. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/262190), or right-click and select Insert a new row. Add one or more rows to the [G3ECOMMIFACE](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/4Gp7g5vbqXez~bEdYaOZHA) table. 
    2. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/262190) or select Insert a new row from the right-mouse menu. Add one or more rows to the [G3E_REPORT](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/~2VhQpRQSi_R90iNba9YSg) table to configure a report. In the G3E_PARAMETER1 field, type the object ID for the Customer Assignment interface object that is used to retrieve assignment information. 
    3. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/262190) to commit the changes to the database. 
  2. In the Metadata Explorer tree view, select the Finds, Queries, Traces, and Reports > Reporting > Reports node. 
    1. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/262190), or right-click and select Insert a new row. Add one or more rows to the [G3E_REPORT](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/~2VhQpRQSi_R90iNba9YSg) table to configure a report. 
    2. In the G3E_USERNAME and G3E_DESCRIPTION fields, type a username and description for the report. 
    3. In the G3E_RINO field, select a report interface from the drop-down list. The HTML report interface is normally used. 
    4. In the G3E_INTERFACEARGUMENT field, click the Ellipsis and supply interface arguments as required. The report interface must accept an XML file as input. 
    5. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/262190) to commit the changes to the database. 
  3. In the Metadata Explorer tree view, select the Finds, Queries, Traces, and Reports > Reporting > Report Mapping by Report node. 
    1. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/262190), or right-click and select Insert a new row. Add one or more rows to the [G3E_REPORTMAPPING](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/gTE5K~kT9KX2yH7cssn59w) table to define the queries that use this report as output. 
    2. In the G3E_RPNO field, select the report you defined in Step 2 from the drop-down list. 
    3. In the G3E_TYPE field, select View Pairs from the drop-down list. 
    4. Select values from the drop-down list in other fields as required.
    5. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/262190) to commit the changes to the database.

### Copy Attributes Command
The user can [copy attributes between features](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/scGyOiqi_Ho2apwB62sl8g) of the same type (FNO) and can copy attributes from one feature to a single feature or to multiple features. However, the user can copy only those attribute values that you define as copyable. 
  * To set the attributes to copy between features:


  1. In the Metadata Explorer tree view, select Core Schema Control > Components and Attributes > <Attribute Name> > Attributes >, select the attribute you want to edit, and set the [G3E_ATTRIBUTE.G3E_COPYATTRIBUTE](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/7SEquKvasMNJcZ25A9H4yw) field to Yes (1) for the attributes you want the command to copy. 
  2. In the \GTechnology\PLSQL\ltt folder, install the UserCopyAttributes.sql package. This database package does the copying when the Copy Feature Attributes command is run. 
SQL> usercopyattributes.sql; 
  3. Optional: If you have written a functional interface that should fire when this component is updated, modify the UserCopyAttributes package to duplicate the logic in the functional interface.

[Common Attribute Edit](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/SUmelf6bi7yknRfMOIMyvA)

### Copying Features
A user can copy an existing feature and create new instances using the Copy Feature command. The command allows user to copy any feature that is specified in metadata (G3E_FEATURE.G3E_COPY = Yes (1)). 
Copy Feature does the following: 
  * Copies all the components that are specified in metadata (G3E_FEATURECOMPONENT.G3E_COPY = Yes (1)). 
  * Copies all the attributes that are specified in metadata (G3E_ATTRIBUTE.G3E_COPY = Yes (1)). 
  * Copies all the attributes that are specified in metadata (G3E_ATTRIBUTE.G3E_COPYATTRIBUTE = Yes (1)). 
  * Creates new instances when the user clicks on the Map. 
  * Tries to establish relationships with the features in vicinity.
  * If Feature Explorer is not visible, new instances are auto saved. 


Copy Feature Behavior
  * By default, if a Feature is specified in metadata as (G3E_FEATURE.G3E_COPY = Yes (1)), all its required components are marked (G3E_FEATURECOMPONENT.G3E_COPY = Yes (1)).* 
  * By default, if an attribute has G3E_COPY or G3E_COPYATTRIBUTE flag set to true, its parent component is marked for Copy.* 
  * By default, if a component is marked for copy, its parent feature is marked for copy.*
  * If the source feature does not have an attribute value set, the default value is assigned.
  * The source feature attribute value takes precedence over the default value.
  * If required attributes or components are marked as G3E_COPY = No (0). The Feature will still get created, but Post Job edits will fail until all the required data is provided. 
  * Copy Feature considers components and attributes from only the current active window during copy. For example, if the active window is a map window, only the components and attributes of that window will be copied. Similarly, if the active window is a detail window, only the components and attributes of that detail window will be copied. 
  * The user can select a non-graphic feature from Feature Explorer to copy and create a new instance. However, it is recommended to mark non-graphic features as G3E_COPY = No(0), which cannot establish relationships with graphic features. 
  * Copied features can always use Reestablish Relationship to establish relationship with other graphic features. 
* This state is set only during the database upgrade process for Copy Feature functionality. For any new feature, component, or attribute addition, NetWorks Core Administrator must manually update the G3E_COPY flag. The default value for G3E_FEATURE.G3E_COPY and G3E_FEATURECOMPONENT.G3E_COPY or G3E_ATTRIBUTE.G3E_COPY is No(0). 
![Note](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/1183626) Labels and styles of a new instance may vary from the source feature, based upon components and attributes marked for copy. 


Copy Feature Workflow
  * To copy an existing feature:


  1. Select a feature and invoke Edit > Features > Copy. Make sure an active job is present. 
  2. Choose the anchor points on source feature by selecting the handle. Once the anchor points are selected, geometries are added to dynamics. 
![CopyFeature_AnchorPoints](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/1183626)
  3. Click on the map to create a new instance. If Feature Explorer is not visible, auto save mode is activated. The instance gets auto saved, and the new instance placement begins immediately. If Feature Explorer is visible, the user can edit any attribute value, then click Save Edits and Continue in Feature Explorer to save the instance and begin its placement. Click Save Edits to save the instance and exit the command. Click Cancel Edits to discard the instance and exit the command. 
  4. Press ESC to exit the command.


![Note](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/1183626) The administrator can change the G3E_COPY flag value as per the requirements.

### Damage Assessment Command

#### Damage Assessment Metadata
The FNO of the damage assessment feature must be specified in the [G3E_INSPECTIONIFACE](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/Wh3GewAqL9Mk80idE_JUQg) metadata table. The damage assessment feature typically has the following components: 
  * A primary attribute component
  * A primary graphic component (area)
  * A damage assessment component (repeating, attribute)
  * A feature class camage component (repeating, attribute)


The FNO of damage assessment feature, CNO of attribute component, CNO of damage assessment component, and CNO of feature class damage component are specified in the [G3E_INSPECTIONIFACE](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/Wh3GewAqL9Mk80idE_JUQg) metadata table. 
DamageAssessmentFID Table Structure  
|  Column Name  |  Description  |  Unique  |  Null  |  PK  |  FK  |  Type  |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |  
|  G3E_FID  |  Unique feature identifier  |  Yes  |  No  |  Yes  |  No  |  Number (9,0)  |  
|  SESSIONID  |  Identifier of the Oracle session  |  No  |  No  |  No  |  No  |  Number(9,0)  |  
The command executes the G3E_ComputePercentDamage procedure in the database, sending the G3E_FNO and G3E_FID of the damage assessment feature and the date, so that it is same for all records inserted by this command. 
The G3E_ComputePercentDamage procedure stored in the database actually computes the percent damage. One damage assessment record is added each time this procedure is run. For each damage assessment, one feature class damage record is created per inspectable/related feature type. 
The G3E_ComputePercentDamage procedure assumes the existence of an initial damage assessment record with G3E_CID=1 and a corresponding initial Feature Class Damage record for each inspectable and/or related feature type containing the count of that feature in the damage assessment area (Total Count) and the initial guess at Percent Total Damage. It uses the FIDs of the inspection features within that damage assessment feature contained in the table defined by the Damage Assessment FIDs record in the G3E_INSPECTIONIFACE table of the inspection features within that damage assessment feature. 
For each inspectable and or related feature type, the procedure determines the following:
  * How many have been inspected (Inspected Count)
  * How many have deficiencies (Deficiency Count)


And computes:
  * PercentInspected (Inspected Count/Total Count)
  * PercentInspectedDamaged (Deficiency Count/Inspected Count)
  * PercentTotalDamage (Deficiency Count/Total Count) — This is the tally so far.


The procedure then updates the damage assessment feature's repeating FeatureClassDamage component, adding a record for each inspectable and related feature class. 
The Damage Assessment command cleans out the DAMAGEASSESSMENTFIDS table once the G3E_ ComputePercentDamage procedure is run. 
Related Topic
[Damage Assessment](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/4TooRJN7T_BOhFDcyXUq0A)

### Import Features Command
The [Import Features](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/WIshk92ns92plaH~JDy~oQ) command allows the user to import features interactively from an input data source. Import files are typically ASCII, but the format is defined by the import object. 
To interpret the ASCII file and to use the input Feature Loader interface object to create the feature, you must create an [IGTImportFeature interface](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/febj4h1vS8jhIYPWolfSyA). The interface can create any kind of feature—point, linear, polygon, and so forth. 
The Import Features command requires definitions in the [G3E_FEATUREIMPORT](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/bcCkgbpY6H2cj2n2TP2TjA) metadata table. Metadata can be [configured for Feature Import](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/siHnpyLxZ2Hz7PE4ZQ~Nig) for either a new schema or an existing schema.

### Insert Legend Command
The [Insert Legend command](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/tBlyeo1mCWt~fHdH~Gj37A) works without configuration; however, users might find that the styles for the legend title and legend key descriptions are not adequate. You can use [Metadata Explorer](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/UTqIHC3d83TOn0KP~nqHeg) to configure two areas of the legend: 
  * The text styles for the legend title and legend entry key descriptions. Create text styles so that users can easily find suitable text styles in the Title and Style fields on the Insert Legend dialog box. 
  * The content of the legend entry key descriptions so that they make sense on the legend. Users do not have to manually edit each legend entry key description. 


The steps in the following workflow are optional.
  * To configure styles for Insert Legend:


  1. Verify that the styles you want to use are set [for use with plot redlines](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/9VpaS6vw9LwAYX9NprEfag). 
  2. [Define a new text style](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/CpXL2BFXY4jhHmnoqlMLZA) or edit an existing style to use as a legend title. For example, type Legend Title as the G3E_USERNAME so it is easy for users to find in the Insert Legend dialog box Title field. 
  3. Repeat Step 2 to create a text style—for example, Legend Entry Description—so it is easy for users to find in the Insert Legend dialog box Style field. 
  4. Create more readable content for legend key descriptions:
    1. In the Metadata Explorer tree view, select the Graphic Display > Styles Rules > <Rule Name> > Rule Steps > <Rule Step> node to update the G3E_STYLERULE table. 
    2. In the G3E_DESCRIPTION field, edit the text so that it makes sense on the legend.
This text is defaulted from the G3E_xxxxSTYLE.G3E_USERNAME field of a normalized table where the G3E_SNO field matches the G3E_STYLERULE.G3E_SNO field. 
![Note](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/258401?tocId=GXPCYUMhrkTgLwQXvSllWQ) You can create a new point, area, or line style with a username that is more readable and [link it to a style rule](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/q4dl7dWIs5NZfqbJsgqufQ). 
    3. To see where the text in the G3E_DESCRIPTION field comes from, double-click the G3E_SNO field (the foreign key).

### Quick Search Command
A user can locate features using the Quick Search command. Quick Search uses pre-existing queries that are mapped to the search types listed in the command. 
  * To associate existing queries to Quick Search search types:


  1. In the [G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/GgvjmZe3GPS7lKO18R6YsQ) table, check that the search names in G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_USERNAME are unique and meaningful. 
  2. For each single argument query that should be included in Quick Search, set the G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_QUICKSEARCH value to 1. This makes the queries available in Quick Search. 
  3. Define the G3E_ANO values for [G3E_FIND](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/k34upujY7Schco2~q76sMQ) and [G3E_FINDCOMPONENT](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/owAcB8aWk48hZOjxW4p9eg) fields G3E_INFORAMTIONALANO1 and G3E_INFORMATIONALANO2. These fields are included to include values that are meaningful to the user. They are added to the select statement and shown in the search results. 


Supported Find and Query Types
Only single argument Finds and Queries from these current commands are supported in the Search tool. 
Find Feature
  * A single argument query is defined as G3E_FIND.G3E_CNO2 is NULL.
  * G3E_FIND.G3E_ANO1 is the single attribute to filter on.
  * SQL select statement that should be run and is generated based on G3E_FIND.G3E_CNO1, G3E_FIND.G3E_ANO1, and G3E_FIND.G3E_INFORMATIONANO1. 
  * If Area is checked, the query is modified to accommodate the active Area of Interest. The current FNO is used for populating the AOI filtered records and stored in the AOIQUERYRESULT table. These records are now inputs to the new modified SQL query. 
  * G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_USERNAME default value is <Feature User Name> by <Attribute User Name>. This value may be changed to a more meaningful name if the default is not adequate. 
Example: Pole by Material
  * Like operator is used in the generated SQL statement that performs a contains comparison of the user specified value and the values in the database. 
  * The active area can be used for spatial filtering


Find Component
  * A single argument query is defined as G3E_FINDCOMPONENT.G3E_CNO2 is NULL.
  * G3E_FINDCOMPATTRIBUTE.G3E_ANO is the single attribute to filter on.
  * SQL select statement that should be run and is generated based on G3E_FINDCOMPONENT.G3E_CNO1, G3E_FINDCOMPATTRIBUTE.G3E_ANO, G3E_FINDCOMPONENT.G3E_INFORMATIONALANO1. 
  * If Area is checked, the query is modified to accommodate the active AOI. The G3E_FEATURE COMPS_OPTABLE is used to retrieve the FNOs that have this component. This list of FNOs is used for populating the AOL filtered records and stored in the AOIQUERYRESULT table. These records are now inputs to the new modified SQL query. 
  * G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_USERNAME default value is <Component User Name> by <Attribute User Name>. This value may be changed to a more meaningful name if the default is not adequate. 
Example: Common by Feature Identifier
  * Like operator is used in the generated SQL statement that performs a contains comparison of the user specified value and the values in the database. 
  * The active area can be used for filtering.


Find Quick Reference
  * A single argument Quick Reference query is defined as
    * G3E_FINDQUICK.G3E_SQL does not contain any optional arguments
    * G3E_FINDQUICKATTRIBUTE.G3E_NULL is 0
    * G3E_FINDQUICKATTRIBUTE.G3E_ANO is greater than 0
    * G3E_FINDQUICKATTRIBUTE contains a single row for G3E_FINDQUICK.FQNO
Query for identifying single argument Quick Reference Finds.
select a.G3E_FQAROWNO, a.g3e_fqno,a.g3e_ano,a.G3E_REFERENCEORDINAL ,b.g3e_sql
from g3e_findquickattribute a , g3e_findquick b
where a.g3e_fqno in (select g3e_fqno from g3e_findquickattribute group by g3e_fqno having count(*)=1) and
a.g3e_fqno=b.g3e_fqno and b.g3e_sql not like '%*/%' and a.g3e_ano>0 and a.g3e_null = 0;
  * G3E_FINDQUICKATTRIBUTE.G3E_ANO is the single attribute to filter on.
  * The SQL select statement that is run is defined in G3E_FINDQUICK.G3E_SQL.
  * G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_USERNAME default value is G3E_FINDQUICK.G3E_USERNAME. This value may be changed to a more meaningful name if the default is not adequate. 
  * Operators used are defined in G3E_FINDQUICK.G3E_SQL.
  * Find Quick Reference does not support usage of Active Area.
  * Find Quick Reference may be configured to require an Area of Interest Location Identifier. The Location Identifier for the query comes from the active Area of Interest. If the query requires a Location Identifier, but no Area of Interest with a Location Identifier is set, the query will not run. 


Attribute Query Simple
  * A single argument Simple Query is defined as
    * G3E_ATTRIBUTEQUERY.G3E_SQL does not contain any optional arguments
    * G3E_SIMPLEQUERYATTRIBUTE.G3E_NULL is 0
    * G3E_ G3E_SIMPLEQUERYATTRIBUTE.G3E_ANO is greater than 0
    * G3E_ G3E_SIMPLEQUERYATTRIBUTE contains a single row for G3E_ATTRIBUTEQUERY.FQNO
select a.G3E_SQAROWNO, a.G3E_AQNO, a.G3E_ANO, b.g3e_username
from G3E_SIMPLEQUERYATTRIBUTE a, G3E_ATTRIBUTEQUERY b
where a.g3e_aqno=b.g3e_aqno and 
a.g3e_aqno in (select g3e_aqno from G3E_SIMPLEQUERYATTRIBUTE group by g3e_aqno having count(*)=1) and 
g3e_sql not like '%*/%' and 
g3e_ano>0 and a.g3e_null=0;
  * G3E_SIMPLEQUERYATTRIBUTE.G3E_ANO is the single attribute to filter on.
  * The SQL select statement that is run is defined in G3E_ATTRIBUTEQUERY.G3E_SQL.
  * This SQL statement is run as is. It is up to the administrator to ensure that G3E_ATTRIBUTEQUERY.G3E_SQL is valid SQL and executes successfully.G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_USERNAME default value is G3E_ATTRIBUTEQUERY.G3E_USERNAME. This value may be changed to a more meaningful name if the default is not adequate. 
  * If Area is checked, the query is modified to accommodate the active AOI. 
    * The G3E_QUERYMAPPING_OPTABLE is used to retrieve the FNOs that have this component when the G3E_ATTRIBUTEQUERY.G3E_AOI field is set to 1. This list of FNOs is used for populating the AOI filtered records and stored in the AOIQUERYRESULT table. These records are now inputs to the new modified SQL query. 
    * When G3E)ATTRIBUTEQUERY.G3E_AOI is set to 0, the G3E_FEATURECOMPS_OPTABLE is used to retrieve the FNOs that have this component. This list of FNOs is used for populating the AOI filtered records and stored in the AQIQUERYRESULT table. 
  * Operators used are defined in G3E_ATTRIBUTEQUERY.G3E_SQL.


Active Area Support
The Quick Search command can be enhanced by including spatial filtering. NetWorks Core provides the utility to handle the areas through Area Manager. The active area can be used as a spatial filter for Quick Search. 
  * To allow use of the Active Area:


  1. If an Active Area is required for a query, configure the pre-existing query with G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_AOI set to 1 and G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_AOILI set to 0. This sets the Active Area as a required parameter when the query is executed. 
  2. If an Active Area is optional for a query, configure the pre-existing query with G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_AOI set to 0 and G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_AOILI set to 0. The user can choose whether to set an Active Area for spatial filtering. 


![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/814910) Find Quick Reference does not support Active Area. 
Location Identifier
Pre-existing queries support attribute filtering based on location identifier. Queries must be configured with G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_AOILI set to 1 and G3E_ANALYSISMAPPING.G3E_AOI set to 0.

### Replace Feature Command

#### Replace Feature Relationship Processing
The Replace Feature command transfers relationships from the original feature to the new feature. In some cases, the relationship is explicitly established; in other cases, the relationship is established when specific attributes are copied. Each relationship type is discussed below. 
Ownership
  * If the feature being replaced is a parent (G3E_RELATIONSHIP.G3E_SUBORDINATE=0), each existing child feature is explicitly related to the new parent feature. There is no additional metadata to configure for parent features. 
  * If the feature being replaced is a child, the parent relationship is transferred when relationship attributes are copied from the source feature to the new feature. Configure the following metadata so that relationships are properly copied: 
Simple Ownership
    * G3E_FEATURECOMPONENT.G3E_REPLACE=1 for the component with owner ID fields identified in G3E_OWNERSHIP.G3E_OWNERFIELD and G3E_OWNERSHIP.G3E_SECONDOWNERFIELD. 
    * G3E_ATTRIBUTE.G3E_EXCLUDEFROMREPLACE=0 for owner ID fields.
Many-to-Many Ownership
    * G3E_FEATURECOMPONENT.G3E_REPLACE=1 for the common component (identified by G3E_RELATIONSHIP.G3E_SUPPORTCNO) with G3E_OWNERFNO AND G3E_OWNERFID fields. 
    * G3E_ATTRIBUTE.G3E_EXCLUDEFROMREPLACE=0 for G3E_OWNERFNO AND G3E_OWNERFID fields.


Node-Ordered Connectivity
  * If the feature being replaced is a node feature, each existing related feature is explicitly related to the new node feature. There is no additional metadata to configure for node features. 
  * If the feature being replaced is an edge (linear) feature, relationships are transferred when relationship attributes are copied from the source feature to the new feature. Configure the following metadata so that relationships are properly copied: 
    * G3E_FEATURECOMPONENT.G3E_REPLACE=1 for the common component (identified by G3E_RELATIONSHIP.G3E_SUPPORTCNO) with these attributes: IN_FNO, IN_FID, OUT_FNO, OUT_FID. 
    * G3E_ATTRIBUTE.G3E_EXCLUDEFROMREPLACE=0 for the same attributes: IN_FNO, IN_FID, OUT_FNO, OUT_FID. 


Node-Edge Connectivity
  * Relationships are transferred when relationship attributes are copied from the source feature to the new feature. Configure the following metadata so that relationships are properly copied: 
    * G3E_FEATURECOMPONENT.G3E_REPLACE=1 for the common component (identified by G3E_RELATIONSHIP.G3E_SUPPORTCNO) with the NODE1_ID and NODE2_ID fields. 
    * G3E_ATTRIBUTE.G3E_EXCLUDEFROMREPLACE=0 for the NODE1_ID and NODE2_ID fields.


Details
  * Relationships are transferred when relationship attributes are copied from the source feature to the new feature. Configure the following metadata so that relationships are properly copied: 
    * G3E_FEATURECOMPONENT.G3E_REPLACE=1 for the component identified by G3E_DETAIL.G3E_ATTRIBUTECNO.
    * G3E_ATTRIBUTE.G3E_EXCLUDEFROMREPLACE=0 for the attribute identified by G3E_DETAIL.G3E_IDENTIFIERANO.

### Transfer Units Command

#### Transfer Units Metadata
The Transfer Units Metadata command has several requirements for the source feature: 
  * The feature-component combinations should be transferable according to the metadata table definition. However, the receiving feature does not have to have an instance of the transfer component. If it does not, one is created. 
  * The source feature should have more than one component of transfer unit to transfer. If the feature has only one unit, the command displays the source feature in the user interface, and an error message states that the user cannot transfer the last unit from a feature. 
  * The command lists the primary transfer unit. If the source feature contains the secondary transfer units that are associated to the primary ones, the command transfers them, but as with primary units, the source feature must have more than one secondary unit. The [G3E_TRANSFER](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/u3HaNjIu_ruhkOpKNvFcsQ) metadata table defines the primary and secondary transfer units. 


Before you can transfer units, a metadata lookup table must be defined to identify features from which data can be transferred, components that can move (primary), and components that must move with these components (secondary); for example, audit or history records. The package UNITTRANSFER must be installed in the Oracle database to complete the actual move and copy work.

### Translate State Command

#### Translate State Metadata
These are the metadata tables associated with Translate State. 
  * G3E_JOBDEFINITION
Set the [G3E_JOBDEFINITION.G3E_JOBSTATEFIELD](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/TBQDr_BsRYh8ej2Rr97t2g) to the name of the field in your job table that holds the state for each job. 
  * G3E_WORKMGMT 
    * Populate a row in [G3E_WORKMGMT](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/KME_1L76HZEDZ5lzihAbeQ) with G3E_TYPE='LifeCycle'. This entry defines the table and optimized table containing the definitions of each possible feature state. Populate that table with the definitions of your feature states. 
    * Populate a row in G3E_WORKMGMT with G3E_TYPE= 'Transitions' that specifies the table and optimized table containing the allowed feature state transitions. Populate that table with the set of allowed transitions. 
    * Populate a row in G3E_WORKMGMT with G3E_TYPE='Feature'. This record's G3E_SUPPORTCNO field specifies the component number of the common component where the feature state is stored for each feature, and the G3E_SUPPORTANO field specifies the attribute number where the feature's state is stored. 
    * Populate a row in G3E_WORKMGMT with G3E_TYPE='JobIdentifier' that identifies the attribute number where the feature's job identifier is stored. This attribute must be stored in a common component of all features whose state is translated. 


Translate State Post Processing Procedures
Functional interfaces do not execute during the Translate State command. However, a post-process procedure is invoked after this operation. In this post processing procedure, you can implement your own business rules required for such edits. When this procedure is called, the state change has been saved in the database, and you have an opportunity to apply other business rules within the same transaction. 
The command calls the USERTRANSLATEFEATURESTATE procedure that in turn calls the G3ETRANSLATEFEATURESTATEPKG. This, in turn, calls the Translate FeatureState procedure. By default, the TranslateFeatureState procedure does not do anything. It is delivered in the \GTechnology\PLSQL\LTT\ translatefeaturestatepkg.sql file. An example implementation is provided in translatefeaturestateexamplepkg.sql. 
procedure TRANSLATEFEATURESTATE (  
FeatureIDs in oFeatureIDs  
);   
oFeatureIDs is a table with one field, defined as Number (10)

## Configuration and Performance Considerations

### Connection Considerations
Not only does NetWorks Core log in to the database, it also finds and opens the DDC files to respond to display requests. The following things affect performance: 
  * Number of component views. This can be more important than the number of DDC files. Each component view published into the DDC has the following: 
    * A schema (column names and column types)
    * A [quad-tree (spatial) index](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/259937)
Provides pointers into the DDC data based on spatial location. 
    * An index on G3E_FID
When the DDC file is opened, the software reads information about these items from the file and keeps track of this information to quickly support display requests. Therefore, a configuration with 1000 component views takes longer to start than one with 250 component views. 
  * DDC location. The node hosting the DDC serves as a file server. Its location relative to the user affects the performance of graphic data fetches. This is a hardware and/or network consideration. The number of users sharing that same DDC location also affects performance. A DDC server with 25 users working simultaneously performs better than with 100 users. 


![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/259937) To prevent conflict between Oracle access and DDC access, do not put the DDC on the same node as the Oracle server.

### Display Performance Considerations
Display performance is the combination of the volume of data requested and the speed of the communications. Your [DDC files](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/20gsQWJ5jm5zeNY1z_rjBw) should be accessible to the client software over a local area network (LAN) supporting at least 10-megabit transfer rates. 
Many factors can affect the volume of data requested, how it is processed, and thus performance: 
  * Too much data displayed at a given display scale
Often, detailed data displays at a small scale, such as 1:5000, when it should not appear until 1:500. Conversely, a lot of data should turn off when the user reaches larger scales, such as 1:500. 
  * Too many legend entries on a legend
The software constructs each legend entry it finds in metadata; so 150 legend entries open faster than 750. This also affects the speed of changing jobs because the software closes and reopens legend entries. System designers should target a maximum of 500 legend entries per display. If you have a requirement for a larger number of legend entries, you should be sure the client machine has sufficient memory to achieve acceptable performance levels. 
  * The number of columns selected into the [component view](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/049MKIFVrB5oBq4DAinIGw)
Nongraphic attributes are required as part of the component view. These attributes are used to determine how the geometry is rendered and to provide the user with the ability to construct ad hoc views using the Display Control filtering capabilities. This functionality can affect both display performance and publishing. The more data you have to process, the more time it takes. 
Component views should contain only the columns necessary to support the user workflows. These are typically for display, relationships, and tooltip identification. 
You should also consider using numeric codes instead of text strings for controlling style selection to reduce the DDC size and to improve the performance of the style rule execution. If text fields are required, use the Oracle Varchar2 data type. With this data type, only the actual characters used are stored in the DDC, not the maximum possible number of characters. 
  * Legend entry filtering
Use metadata legend display filters to generate specialized output products and/or custom maps for interactive viewing. When a single table in the model contains data that requires user display control or needs to be represented with different styles, use [synthesized components](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/BHztsPXCkqRWc8ufJn_Dkg). If you design multiple legend entries that access the same component view but with a different filter, the display system must access and process the same component view multiple times for that display range, once for each legend entry, filtering out the unwanted records 
  * The number and complexity of filters in a style rule or a label rule
The concern about filter complexity is the same as for filtering legends. The number of filters needed to determine the symbology and label contents also affects display time. It is important to order these by probability of success, with the most probable first. It is faster to display a feature if it satisfies the first filter than if it satisfies the fifteenth. To speed up the display, optimize component views for style Id (field G3E_STYLEID), the label format (field G3E_LABELFORMAT), or both. 
  * Details that overlap
The display of one detail must filter out the records of the overlapping details (like legend entry filtering). It is important to keep details from overlapping. 
  * A component view containing many large features that cover a large extent (boundaries, hydrography, streets) as well as features of small extent
Boundary features, for example, typically have a hierarchical structure; that is, countries contain states, which contain counties. If all of this data are published into a single view, the country polygon resides in the root node of the spatial index, high in the quad tree. The state nodes typically reside at one of the intermediate nodes in the index, and the bulk of the county data should be stored in the leaf nodes. When the system attempts to process this boundary data, the country boundary is retrieved for every action associated with boundaries. Even after a user zooms in to a very small area, the DDC navigates those entries because its range overlaps the display area. Then, it is discarded because the geometry does not actually intersect the display area. It is important to structure the data so the graphic data are stored in the leaf nodes of the quad tree. In this case, creating new features or using synthesized components to separate these large features from the small features is helpful. See [Synthesized Components](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/BHztsPXCkqRWc8ufJn_Dkg) for more information. 
  * Display data at a much smaller scale than that for which it was originally captured
For example, displaying a feature at 1:10000 when the original data source was intended to display at 1:500. At 1:10000, a user cannot distinguish a large percentage of the coordinates, so they do not contribute to the picture. Thus, time is expended processing the coordinates for no gain. The data could be thinned to reduce volume during display. 
  * Display features at a large scale even though they cover very large areas
If a large provincial boundary needs to be displayed at 1:500, all the data in its very high quad node is processed even though very little displays. Substituting many small linear features for the large features' boundaries can yield the correct display without the expense of processing the larger volume of data.

### Incremental Publishing Considerations
Frequent data publishing lets you delete master delta records (ltt_id=0) from the MODIFICATIONLOG, which reduces the size of the table and the index, in addition to reducing the amount of work to exercise queries against it. If a full data publish is too time-consuming to publish frequently, use [incremental data publish](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/KMyb7We6CN6SLJS3Anpyuw) to reduce the time to publish data.

### Maximizing Performance

#### Computing Statistics
The NetWorks Core interface to the Oracle database is based on the expectation that query execution plans are generated by the Cost Based Optimizer (CBO). Accurate and current statistics about the data tables must be available for the CBO to effectively evaluate the cost of an execution plan and select the best one. You must regularly compute statistics and create histograms on all data tables in case they become stale and inaccurate as the table is edited and grows and/or shrinks. 
How often you compute statistics on a table depends on the frequency and volume of changes to the table. You may need to compute statistics on a very busy table, such as a connectivity table, every week or every few days. You may need to recompute statistics on a quiet table, possibly a landbase parcel table, every month or even less often; to do so more often may be wasteful. 
If you do not regularly compute statistics and create histograms, the quality of the execution plan that the CBO generates is suspect, and the query execution may be more expensive than needed. It may use more memory, perform more I/O, and take more time than it otherwise would; and it competes with other Oracle sessions for these resources, slowing everyone down and undermining the scalability of the system. 
You should use the DBMS_STATS package to compute statistics and histograms on your objects. This example computes statistics on all objects and lets Oracle determine the columns on which to collect histograms based on the data distribution of the columns.   
|  Example DBMS_STATS.GATHER_SCHEMA_STATS (OWNNAME=> 'SCHEMAOWNER', METHOD_OPT=>'FOR ALL COLUMNS SIZE SKEWONLY', DEGREE=>7);  |  
| --- |  
This example computes statistics on all objects, specifically computes statistics on indexed columns,and specifies that the histogram have 50 buckets.   
|  Example DBMS_STATS.GATHER_SCHEMA_STATS (NULL,NULL,FALSE,'FOR ALL INDEXED COLUMNS SIZE 50', DBMS_STATS.DEFAULT_DEGREE,'DEFAULT',TRUE,NULL,NULL,'GATHER');  |  
| --- |  
This example operates on a particular object, specifically computes statistics on indexed columns, and specifies that the histogram have 50 buckets.   
|  Example DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS ( NULL, 'TABLE_NAME', NULL, NULL, FALSE, 'FOR ALL INDEXED COLUMNS SIZE 50', DBMS_STATS.DEFAULT_DEGREE, 'DEFAULT', TRUE );  |  
| --- |  
This example operates on a particular table, specifically computes statistics on the LTT_ID column, and specifies that the histogram have 200 buckets.   
|  Example DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS ( NULL, REC.TABLE_NAME, NULL, NULL, FALSE, 'FOR COLUMNS LTT_ID SIZE 200', DBMS_STATS.DEFAULT_DEGREE, 'DEFAULT', TRUE );  |  
| --- |  
Typically, most records in a table are master records and have an LTT_ID of 0. Relatively few records are job records with LTT_ID not equal to 0. It is important for Oracle to know this, because if you query for records with LTT_ID=7, the index on LTT_ID is very helpful. But if you query for records with LTT_ID=0 (for example, publishing master records), it is, in fact, faster to scan the table rather than use the index. 
To regularly recompute statistics and create histograms, you can set up a job to monitor the tables. You must set the MONITORING attribute on the tables you want to monitor. This should consider all facility model tables plus NetWorks Core[ system tables](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/cKG7KdVEYzxfeQ_5955GDw) and metadata tables. You cannot monitor TEMPORARY TABLES. This can be done in the CREATE TABLE or the ALTER TABLE statement, and the attribute is in USER_TABLES. 
This example submits a job to gather stale statistics every night. It only gathers statistics if they were once computed and are now stale. It does not compute statistics on new tables. You must do that first.   
|  Example DBMS_JOB.SUBMIT ( N_JOBNO, 'DBMS_STATS.GATHER_SCHEMA_STATS (NULL,NULL,FALSE,''FOR ALL INDEXED COLUMNS SIZE REPEAT'', DBMS_STATS.DEFAULT_DEGREE,''DEFAULT'',TRUE,NULL,NULL,''GATHER STALE'');', TRUNC(SYSDATE) + 18/24, 'SYSDATE + 1' );  |  
| --- |  
To properly administer your system, you should become familiar with these functions from your Oracle documentation and know how and when to use them.

#### Data Modeling Philosophy
NetWorks Core can be configured to perform many tasks and, for every task added, the application or the database must do work to comply. This flexibility requires you to analyze your data model requirements and the productivity needs of your users. Test your data model with large volumes of data for the most common workflows to measure network and database volume. An SQL statement that appears straightforward for one person to execute is completely different when 200 users are executing it or competing for the same resources. 
Simplify to Avoid Problems
Generally, you can avoid some data model problems by keeping your model and workflows simple. Model how users are going to interact with the system and how they perceive the data. Make sure your model is simple so you do not spend time maintaining something that is not necessary, and verify that the data model is representative of what your users need. Then document what you have done so that it is easier to add workflows and capabilities in the future. 
Example Workflows
Consider the following workflows where the model can help or hinder success: 
Placement
When a [user places a feature](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/YY5WEAfiFC2VOvip1IxW6A), records are inserted into the component tables, and some user action is required for most components (not silently placed ones). The software asks for user input and inserts those records. A feature that inserts five records places faster than one that inserts 20 records. Think about the work that you are asking the system and the user to do. 
If a workflow requires too many steps or if users must wait too long for features to place, they may become frustrated; consider how many component records are required and also how many are typically generated. If only five are required but the user typically creates 10, then 10 is the operative number of records inserted. Consider the actions that you are requiring of the user, which actions are really required and which actions, although providing optional capability, could be defaulted a large percentage of the time. 
Do not make all users and workflows pay a performance penalty just to accommodate special cases. Sometimes distinct components should be consolidated in another component. 
Dialog boxes
When populating or updating attribution for features, place the required and the most frequently used attributes on the first tab. This frees users from searching among various tabs and attributes to find what they want. You can also consolidate the attributes into fewer component records. 
Relationships
As with placement, [relationships cause records to be inserted or updated](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/e2tt5qpeYNY9MM7Wm73iAw) and typically require some user action or input. A feature with one or two relationships is simpler and faster to create than one with 10 or 20. Think about the work that you are asking the system and the user to do. 
Relationships are often defined and established in the model because they represent reality. However, capturing them in the data might not contribute to the business process. Before creating relationships, make sure that having this information helps to streamline the process. Sometimes you can derive the relationship through another set of attribution. If the additional query processing is not time consuming—or if the user needs it only occasionally—it may be more effective to derive the result than to maintain the relationship as an inherent part of the model. 
Find and query
Finds and queries are often defined as workflows but are documented after the model has been defined and approved, requiring complicated SQL to access the required parts of the model. If users execute finds and queries frequently, the complicated SQL statements can hinder performance. 
Some of these SQL statements must join across a number of tables because the model has logically separated the needed or requested information into different tables. If the model can consolidate some of these tables, the resultant query SQL could be simpler and would perform better. 
Views
Views encapsulate SQL so that the SQL formulated by the client is simpler to construct. The resultant SQL in the database is the combination of the view and user SQL. Views are convenient and can be functional, restricting client access to certain rows and columns. 
Views can deceive you into generating more complex SQL than you expect. When you execute SQL against a view, the resultant SQL in the database is the combination of the view and user SQL. This may be more complex than you expected because sometimes a subclause of a predicate shows up multiple times. 
Views are also objects in the database. Every time a view is referenced, Oracle must look it up in the dictionary and check the privileges of the user. Views are a powerful database tool, but use them judiciously. 
Display performance
During display, data are accessed from the DDC for each appropriate legend entry at the specified display scale. The more legend entries you have to display, the more work the software must do to display them. This is sometimes overlooked when designing legends. Consider how the user interacts with the data. Determine what data are required for a given workflow. Maybe a different legend with its own legend entries is appropriate for a different workflow. 
Another capability that can affect display performance is creating multiple legend entries over a single component view but applying different attribute filters to each. This shows as separate items to the user without actually creating separate features—items are distinguished based on attribution. This is functionally correct; however, it causes the display system to access and process the same component view multiple times for that display range—once for each legend entry, filtering out the unnecessary records. It is important to recognize the cost of this design. Creating multiple component views over the same component can improve display performance. See [Synthesized Components](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/BHztsPXCkqRWc8ufJn_Dkg) for more information. 
Symbology is dynamically assigned to components using [style rules](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/q4dl7dWIs5NZfqbJsgqufQ) that test data values from component views published into the DDC. Each [style rule](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/A4cS3c4qexeiByfe4rw2qQ) can exercise multiple tests and assign symbology according to the first test that passes. Thus, style rules should be applied in the order of probability of passing. This minimizes the number of tests that need to be exercised. Creating many style rule tests and ordering them poorly can cause the display system to do unnecessary work. This applies to [label rules](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/D9vkMG6TKLHXXMJCYLzxHg) as well. 
Details
[Details](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/huNn2ZN9Fy0tiVITuoEKRQ) are small amounts of geographic data. NetWorks Core uses details to prevent cluttering the geographic view. These are different components than geographic components and thus different component views. A given detail component view contains records for all the component details. When a user displays a detail window, the component view records are filtered on the detail identifier to eliminate any records from another detail that might overlap this one and fall in the same graphic range. 
The intent of the detail window range is to minimize the overlapping of detail ranges. If detail windows do not overlap much, the display system accesses only records for that detail (and the filtering on detail identifier is redundant). But if details overlap a lot, many records of other details in the graphic range are accessed, only to be filtered out. 
In busy areas, this means that details have a very small graphic range, and the scale at which they are displayed is very different than that of geographic data. This implies that a different legend with different style and label size is needed to display detail data correctly. Therefore, you must keep details from overlapping during data migration . 
Picklists
[Picklists](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/IlbDWhEtofQCqbDOjwdYjQ) allow users to conveniently populate attributes. Picklist filters help by restricting the choices of the user to values that make sense, given attribute values already populated. Filtered picklists are satisfied by querying the database picklist table since the SQL can become complicated. The cost goes up as the picklist filter SQL becomes more complicated. Picklist filters also increase network and database access and can have a noticeable affect on user interaction. 
Business rules
[Triggers](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/a4u3hOioIKZ2wkMqTyAwiw) and [functional](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/V3R13AOaIqDt48GFIejEkg) and [relationship attribute interfaces](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/sy9iZejet2kjZVL5QuFXoA) let you implement specialized rules for your users. This is an opportunity to do some work for the user and to enforce integrity. The performance risk is double because each execution is an added cost, and the implementation of those rules can be done inefficiently, thus adding to the cost. Review all of your business logic for efficiency and affect on database performance. 
Regional subsetting
In a model with [regional subsetting](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/pojLH5IuIFXzS9HmohODXQ), running queries that filter on a subsetting attribute containing the region name can lead to a performance cost. If every single table has this subsetting attribute, the queries are fairly simple. But if a common table carries this subsetting attribute for all features, all queries to other components must join on G3E_FID to this common table. This is done automatically by the LTT views. In this case, every query must pay this performance cost, and it can add up over many users. Component views that join several components together multiply this cost.

#### Database Code Tips
Here are some tips to make your SQL perform better. You must educate yourself about Oracle so that your SQL provides optimum performance.   
|  ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/257493) Here are a few tips regarding database software from Expert One-on-One Oracle by Thomas Kyte, 2001, Wrox Press: 
  * You should do it in a single SQL statement if at all possible.
  * If you cannot do it in a single SQL statement, then do it in PL/SQL.
  * If you cannot do it in PL/SQL, try a Java stored procedure.
  * If you cannot do it in Java, do it in a C external procedure.
  * If you cannot do it in a C external routine, reconsider why you need to do it.

 |  
| --- |  
Some of these tips may seem insignificant, but the results can multiply with the volume of the table and the number of simultaneous users. 
  * Use caution with SQL statements such as the following:
SQL> select from DUAL
Do not use this statement unless absolutely necessary. Dual is an object that has contention just like any busy table. This causes users to wait. 
SQL> select * from TABLE
![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/257493) Using Select * in an application is considered bad practice by Oracle and could crash an application. Additionally, if the table contains a geometry type column, it fails. SQL> select from TABLE where COLUMN when there is no index on that column. 
  * Use caution with SQL statements that perform full table scans. While a full table scan may indeed be the appropriate execution plan, it can be expensive. 
  * Minimize queries to the database.
  * Use bind variables. This radically reduces hard parses and does not fill up the shared pool so quickly. 


For more information about making your database perform better, see [Database Tuning](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/GYg1KlgB3a268EoCnfPyyg).

#### Database Tuning
The performance of your NetWorks Core system greatly depends on the performance of your Oracle database. It is not just a repository to extract and load facility data. It is an engine that performs a lot of work for your NetWorks Core users. That work is carried out using SQL statements and PL/SQL blocks that execute in the database. The configuration and tuning of the Oracle database engine determines how well that SQL is executed. 
The first thing you should check is your INIT.ORA (or SPFILE.ORA) file, which contains parameters that govern much of Oracle's behavior. The following table lists some Oracle parameters and values that provide good performance. The table includes explanations for the more subtle parameters. You should be familiar with Oracle documentation on these parameters and how they affect your database performance. These may not be the best values for your system, but you should be conscientious about setting them.   
|  Oracle Parameter  |  Value  |  Description  |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
|  db_block_size  |  8 KB  |  The size of single- block I/O requests.  |  
|  db_cache_size  |  4 GB  |  Specifies the size of the default cache for the database's standard block size. No definition necessary if ASMM*.   |  
|  db_file_multiblock_read_count  |  8  |  Specifies the number of blocks that are read in a single I/O during a full table scan or index fast full scan.   |  
|  large_pool_size  |  32 MB  |  Specifies the size (in bytes) of the large pool allocation heap. The large pool allocation heap is used in shared server systems for session memory, by parallel execution for message buffers, and by backup processes for disk I/O buffers. No definition necessary if ASMM.   |  
|  log_buffer  |  2 MB  |  Specifies the amount of memory (in bytes) that Oracle uses when buffering redo entries to a redo log file. Redo log entries contain a record of the changes that have been made to the database block buffers.   |  
|  open_cursors  |  1500  |  Specifies the maximum number of open cursors (handles to private SQL areas) a session can have at once.   |  
|  optimizer_dynamic_sampling  |  2  |  Specifies the dynamic sampling level used to determine more accurate selectivity and cardinality estimates for database tables without statistics. NetWorks Core uses temporary tables for some processing, and setting this parameter can help the optimizer choose appropriate execution plans for the SQL referencing those temporary tables.   |  
|  optimizer_index_caching  |  0  |  Between 0 and 100. Indicates the percentage of blocks accessed using indexed access that can be expected to be found in the Buffer Cache. Higher numbers increase the likelihood that indexes are used.   |  
|  optimizer_index_cost_adj  |  100  |  Indicates the percentage cost of physical I/O requests for indexed access compared to full table-scans. Smaller numbers increase the likelihood that indexes are used.   |  
|  optimizer_secure_view_merging   |  FALSE  |  Enables the optimizer to use view merging to improve query performance without performing the checks that would otherwise be performed to ensure that view merging does not violate any security intentions of the view creator. The security check for merging views is not required in NetWorks Core.   |  
|  pga_aggregate_target  |  25% of the size of the SGA_TARGET/DB_CACHE_SIZE  |  Use V$PGASTAT and V$PGA_TARGET_ADVICE to improve Cache Hit Percentage during work loads. See the Oracle Tuning PGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET Help topic for more information. If WORKAREA_SIZE_POLICY is set to MANUAL, Oracle uses SORT_AREA_SIZE which is maintained for backward compatibility.   |  
|  processes  |  500-2,500  |  Based on the number of users and sessions you expect.  |  
|  session_cached_cursors  |  512  |  Number cursors a session can cache. If SQL is executed in a session that matches one of these cursors, it can be used without reopening and with no parsing.   |  
|  sga_max_size  |  min. sga_target, 8 GB  |  ASMM. SGA_MAX_SIZE specifies the maximum size of the SGA for the lifetime of the instance.  |  
|  sga_target  |  4 GB  |  ASMM. If SGA_TARGET is specified, then the following memory pools are automatically sized:
  * Buffer cache (DB_CACHE_SIZE)
  * Shared pool (SHARED_POOL_SIZE)
  * Large pool (LARGE_POOL_SIZE)
  * Java pool (JAVA_POOL_SIZE)

 |  
|  shared_pool_reserved_size  |  128 MB  |  Specifies (in bytes) the shared pool space reserved for large contiguous requests for shared pool memory. You can use this parameter to avoid performance degradation in the shared pool in situations where pool fragmentation forces Oracle to search for and free chunks of unused pool to satisfy the current request. Oracle's default is 5% of the shared_pool_size. 25 to 30% is an improvement because of NetWorks Core uses PL/SQL extensively.   |  
|  shared_pool_size  |  512 MB  |  Specifies (in bytes) the size of the shared pool. The shared pool contains shared cursors, stored procedures, control structures, and other structures. NetWorks Core executes a wide variety of SQL and PL/SQL to do the users' work. Depending on the number of users and their activity, a smaller number tends to cause hard- parsing, which degrades performance. No definition necessary if ASMM.   |  
|  timed_statistics  |  True  |  Enables and disables the collection of timed statistics, such as CPU and elapsed times, by the SQL Trace facility and the collection of various statistics in the dynamic performance tables. The default value of False disables timing. A value of True enables timing. Enabling timing causes extra timing calls for low- level operations. This is a dynamic parameter. It is also a session parameter.   |  
|  undo_management  |  AUTO  |  Automatic Undo management.  |  
|  workarea_size_policy  |  AUTO  |  When set to AUTO, Oracle uses PGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET to govern memory allocated across all database server processes.   |  
*ASMM – Automatic Shared Memory Management
General Performance Notes
  * You should have 4-6 REDO Logs of 10 or 20mb each.
  * You should have 10 Rollback segments.
  * The most common performance problems in NetWorks Core cause inefficient execution plans that consume resources and CPU: 
    * Lack of current statistics 
    * Missing or incorrect indexes 
    * Non-optimal Oracle parameters


Another common performance problem is excessive soft parsing and hard parsing. When an SQL statement is executed, an execution plan (built by the Optimizer) is followed. That execution plan is stored in the shared pool. Building an execution plan (hard parsing) is expensive, so it is a good idea to try to keep them around to be reused (soft parsing). If Oracle can find the SQL statement in the shared pool (soft parse), it can use it and avoid a hard parse (rebuilding the execution plan). 
Haphazard, non-uniform SQL (no bind variables) can exacerbate excessive hard parsing and soft parsing, causing most SQL statements to be unique so that Oracle cannot find them in the shared pool, and then it must hard parse them. This makes the shared pool busier, and more processes have to wait. The shared pool fills up and old SQL statements get kicked out even if they are reuseable. When that same SQL is executed, since it has been kicked out of the shared pool, it bust be hard parsed again. This is very inefficient, causing latch contention, spins, and sleeps on the shared pool and excessive CPU utilization. 
NetWorks Core has made a large effort to minimize this problem. The NetWorks Core variety of SQL typically requires a shared pool of 512 MB. 
It is better to avoid even soft parsing SQL. Each session has a cursor cache where it holds on to frequently executed SQL cursors. If Oracle finds the cursor in this cache, it can use it directly without searching for it in the shared pool. This is called soft-soft parsing and is ideal. The session_cached_cursors parameter indicates how many cursors a session holds onto. Set this to 128 or, even better, 512 to minimize parsing.

#### Large, Busy Tables
Some busy tables in the system grow and shrink with user and administrator activity. These tables can oscillate between hundreds and hundreds of thousands of rows in a very short time. If statistics are computed on such a table when it is very small and if it grows very large more quickly than statistics would normally be recomputed, the CBO is suddenly at a disadvantage when trying to determine query execution plans involving that table. 
To avoid this situation, ensure that the statistics for these tables are such that the Cost Based Optimizer (CBO) generates efficient execution plans. Typically this means that the statistics should reflect a large number of rows, which might cause the CBO to pick a less efficient plan when the table is indeed small. Typically, however, the cost of this is much smaller than the cost of executing a plan built for a small table, when in fact the table is quite large. This is a three-step process: 
  1. Create a table to store these statistics.
DBMS_STATS.CREATE_STAT_TABLE ('SCHEMA_OWNER', 'SAVESTATS');
  2. Export the statistics to the table you created in Step 1.
DBMS_STATS.EXPORT_TABLE_STATS ('SCHEMA_OWNER', 'MODIFICATIONLOG', STATTAB=>'SAVESTATS');
  3. To set or restore statistics, delete the current statistics and import the old statistics.
DBMS_STATS.DELETE_TABLE_STATS('SCHEMA_OWNER', 'MODIFICATIONLOG'); DBMS_STATS.IMPORT_TABLE_STATS ('SCHEMA_OWNER', 'MODIFICATIONLOG', STATTAB => 'SAVESTATS');


These are examples of large, busy tables:
  * MODIFICATIONLOG
  * LTT_UNDO_LOG
  * PENDINGEDITS
  * CONFLICTS


The MODIFICATIONLOG grows to be the largest by far.
These tables are so busy because many users and sessions are inserting, updating, and deleting many records. To improve the parallelism of accessing these tables, create them with five FREELISTS and six Transaction Slots. These are the FREELIST and INITTRANS storage parameters in the CREATE TABLE statement. The FREELIST is managed through a hash list, so it must be a prime number. 
Automatic segment-space management in locally managed tablespaces eliminates the need to specify the PCTUSED, FREELISTS, and FREELIST GROUPS parameters. If possible, switch from manual space management to automatic segment-space management.

#### Normalizing Data
Normalizing your relational database means separating data into groups and defining the right relationships among them. These are the characteristics of a normalized database: 
  * Each piece of data is in only one table.
  * The tables are independent.
  * Only the key relationship exists between tables.


The normalization process helps you understand your data and how it should behave and interact. It gives you insight into the information as you visualize the data, its dependencies, and relationships. You should regard it as part of analysis, not design. 
However, normalization in of itself does not help to improve the speed and efficiency of your tasks, which is the goal of application development. To improve the speed and efficiency of tasks, you must consider how the user performs those tasks — how they think about and interact with the data. While people merely use data, they actually perform tasks, and how they perform those tasks should dictate the organization of data to streamline those tasks. 
Normal Forms
Normal forms come in three levels:
  * First level—Lets you separate data into tables where the data in each table is of a similar type and each row has a primary key (unique identifier). 
  * Second level—Lets you separate repetitious data into other tables (data that is not dependent on the entire key and data that is not solely dependent on the key). 
  * Third level—The entire key and nothing else.


Denormalization
While you design your database to make it more responsive and successful, you can violate the third normal form in the table design by pushing data redundantly into a table where it is not wholly dependent on the primary key. This should not be done lightly. You can write triggers to implement and enforce these rules, and you should not allow users to modify these copied columns. This can make queries run faster by eliminating some joins across multiple tables. 
Make sure that the data model is fully normalized before beginning denormalization.  
|  Examples
  * Include children in the parent record. You should know the number of children.
  * Store a particular child in the parent. The number of children is unknown, but typical access is for the one with a particular attribute—most recent, largest, and so forth. 
  * Hard code static data like Yes and No rather than create a separate table. Full normalization requires a separate table with the Yes and No values. 
  * Store running totals rather than computing sums in many queries.
  * Combine reference tables.
  * If your model generates many reports that overlap but also require many joins, create a report table once, and generate the reports from that table. 
  * Duplicate a key beyond an immediate child.

 |

#### Pursuing Performance Problems
A common pitfall in performance tuning is to mistake the symptoms of a problem for the actual problem. You must recognize that many performance statistics indicate the symptoms and that merely identifying the symptom is not sufficient data to implement a remedy. 
If you are experiencing performance problems and do not know the cause, follow these guidelines: 
Determine whether the performance problem is systemic or specific to a particular action. 
Is the performance problem common to:
  * All users and all activity (database and DDC)—Everything is slow.
    * Your network is overloaded. You can measure network activity with Windows' Performance Monitor (perfmon). 
    * Your hardware is scaled too small. Check your desktop workstations, DDC servers, and database server with the Windows Performance Monitor (perfmon). 
  * All users and all database activity but not DDC activity—Displays are quick but placement, edit, and queries are slow. 
    * Your network is overloaded. You can measure network activity with the Windows Performance Monitor (perfmon). 
    * Your database configuration is not optimized or tuned. [Check the Oracle parameters](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/GYg1KlgB3a268EoCnfPyyg). You can use Oracle Automatic Workload Repository (AWR) or [statspack](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/qNoB6wr09OaYjdFS9o2tuA) to monitor the database and you can use [SQL Trace](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/mJaH2zHPqS568XtrKtxXhw) to look at the activity of a session. 
  * All users and all DDC activity but not database activity—Placement, edit, and queries are quick, but displays are slow. 
    * Your network is overloaded. You can measure network activity with the Windows Performance Monitor (perfmon). 
    * Your DDC server's I/O is inefficient. Check your DDC servers with the Windows Performance Monitor (perfmon). 
    * Your DDC layout is not optimal. See [Configuration and Model Considerations](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/_1Q1vPaMl2hBVCZ3BlQgRw) (Display) and [DDC Restrictions](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/20gsQWJ5jm5zeNY1z_rjBw). 
  * Only certain users and/or workstations are slow.
    * Workstation hardware scaled too small. Check your desktop workstations with the Windows Performance Monitor (perfmon). 
    * Network configuration for that workstation is inefficient. You can measure network activity with the Windows Performance Monitor (perfmon). 
  * Only certain actions or commands are slow.
    * Specific SQL performs poorly. [Turn on diagnostics](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/7xX7B_vERfkLcHh~OUHqFA) for the DataContext object, which logs all SQL executed against the database. After performing the operation that is slow, examine the diagnostics output, and identify the long, slow SQL. Use SQLTrace to look at the execution plan. 
    * If all the SQL performs well, the problem may be that the client workstation hardware is scaled too small for this action. Check desktop workstation activity with the Windows Performance Monitor (perfmon). This may identify a poor NetWorks Core algorithm for your case.

#### Tracing Sessions and Determining SQL Execution Plans

##### The Trace File
The trace file is ASCII, and you can read it with a text editor. If you are running Microsoft Windows and the trace file came from a UNIX system, you may have to open it with Microsoft WordPad to get readable formatting. You may not be able to read trace if you are not in the administrative group for Oracle. You can set the parameter _trace_files_public to True so that all users can read these files, but you may not want to do that for a production environment because these files contain sensitive information. 
The trace file is compact and difficult to read. You can run TKPROF on it to get more readable output, execution plans, and statistics. However, the trace file itself can be useful because it provides a chronological listing of everything that is going on in the database for the session. This can show the fallout of executing an SQL statement. You can see the effect of triggers that may fire, subsequent procedure calls, and all the system SQL that Oracle executes to support the SQL. It also indicates whether a statement was found in the shared pool or whether it had to be hard parsed, which is important information. It includes information on Bind variables and Wait events, which are not propagated to the TKPROF file. 
This is an example of one SQL statement:  
|  Example PARSING IN CURSOR #38 len=64 dep=2 uid=23 oct=3 lid=23 tim=18446744073566733458 hv=4157925779 ad='41f91e70'  Select SWITCH_CENTRE_CLLI from GC_NETELEM where G3E_FID = :B_FID END OF STMT PARSE #38:c=0,e=12208,p=0,cr=32,cu=0,mis=1,r=0,dep=2,og=0,tim=18446744073566733451 BINDS #38:  bind 0: dty=2 mxl=22(21) mal=00 scl=00 pre=00 oacflg=03 oacfl2=1 size=24 offset=0 bfp=032f2de4 bln=22 avl=04 flg=05  value=347668 EXEC #38:c=15625,e=5636,p=0,cr=0,cu=0,mis=0,r=0,dep=2,og=4,tim=18446744073566739227 FETCH #38:c=0,e=435,p=0,cr=4,cu=0,mis=0,r=1,dep=2,og=4,tim=18446744073566739699 STAT #38 id=1 cnt=1 pid=0 pos=1 obj=0 op='FILTER (cr=4 r=0 w=0 time=420 us)' STAT #38 id=2 cnt=1 pid=1 pos=1 obj=9848 op='TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID B$GC_NETELEM (cr=4 r=0 w=0 time=64 us)'  STAT #38 id=3 cnt=1 pid=2 pos=1 obj=9850 op='INDEX RANGE SCAN IDX_B$GC_NETELEM_FID (cr=3 r=0 w=0 time=46 us)'  STAT #38 id=4 cnt=0 pid=1 pos=2 obj=0 op='NESTED LOOPS (cr=0 r=0 w=0 time=0 us)' STAT #38 id=5 cnt=0 pid=4 pos=1 obj=0 op='COLLECTION ITERATOR PICKLER FETCH (cr=0 r=0 w=0 time=0 us)'  STAT #38 id=9 cnt=0 pid=8 pos=1 obj=9852 op='INDEX RANGE SCAN IDX_B$GC_NETELEM_LTTID (cr=0 r=0 w=0 time=0 us)'  STAT #38 id=11 cnt=0 pid=10 pos=1 obj=9851 op='INDEX RANGE SCAN IDX_B$GC_NETELEM_G3EID (cr=0 r=0 w=0 time=0 us)'  STAT #38 id=12 cnt=1 pid=1 pos=2 obj=0 op='COLLECTION ITERATOR PICKLER FETCH (cr=0 r=0 w=0 time=6 us)'  This shows the actual SQL statement because it is building the execution plan.  
 |  Text   |  Description  |  
| --- | --- |  
|  PARSING IN CURSOR #38  |  The cursor number is 38  |  
|  len=64  |  Length of SQL statement is 64 characters.  |  
|  dep=2  |  Recursive depth of the cursor. In this case it was not from the client, but from a trigger or procedure one level down. Recursive SQL is SQL perfomed on behalf of some other SQL. Typically this is SQL executed by Oracle to parse a query or perform space management. It can also be caused by PLSQL.   |  
|  uid=23  |  Schema user ID of parsing user. This may be different than the LID below, especially if the application altered the session to set the current_schema to change the parsing schema.   |  
|  oct=3  |  Oracle command type   |  
|  lid=23  |  Privilege user ID used to security-check the acess privileges against.   |  
|  tim=18446744073566733458  |  Timestamp. As of Oracle9i some times are available to microsecond accuracy (1/1,000,000th of a second). The timestamp can be used to determine times between points in the trace file. The value is the value in V$TIMER when the line was written. If there are TIMESTAMPS in the file you can use the difference between 'tim' values to determine an absolute time.   |  
|  hv=4157925779  |  Hash ID  |  
|  ad='41f91e70'  |  SQLTEXT address (see <View:V$SQLAREA> and <View:V$SQLTEXT>)  |  
 |  
If the statement being executed already has an execution plan, you do not see the Parsing line or the SQL, just the Bind, Exec, and Fetch lines. If you were tracing the session when Cursor #21 was first parsed, you can search backward and find the Parsing statement, the SQL, and information on the execution plan. 
The Exec line displays the execution of SQL (determining the rows of the answer). 
The Fetch line displays the actual fetching of rows from a cursor. 
For the Parse, Exec, and Fetch operations:   
|  Text  |  Description  |  
| --- | --- |  
|  c  |  CPU time in hundredths of a second.  |  
|  e  |  Elapsed time   |  
|  p  |  Number of physical reads performed.  |  
|  cr   |  Number of blocks read in consistent (query) mode (logical I/O).  |  
|  cu  |  Number of blocks retrieved in current mode.  |  
|  mis  |  Cursor missed in the cache. If this is 1, then it was not found in the shared pool and had to be hard parsed.   |  
|  r  |  Number of rows processed.  |  
|  dep  |  Recursive call depth (0 = user SQL, >0 = recursive).  |  
|  og  |  Optimizer goal:  1=All_Rows 2=First_Rows 3=Rule 4=Choose   |  
|  tim  |  Timestamp (large number in 100ths of a second). Use this to determine the time between any two operations.   |  
The STAT line reports explain plan statistics for the numbered cursor. These let you know the 'run time' explain plan.   
|  Text  |  Description  |  
| --- | --- |  
|  Id  |  Line of the explain plan which the row count applies to (starts at line 1). This is effectively the row source row count for all row sources in the execution tree.   |  
|  Cnt  |  Number of rows for this row source.  |  
|  Pid   |  Parent id of this row source.  |  
|  Pos  |  Position in explain plan.  |  
|  Obj  |  Object id of row source (if this is a base object).   |  
|  op=  |  The row source access operation. This is a row in the execution plan. This is shown better after you TKPROF the file and when there is more on execution plans in that section.   |  
The BIND lines show values of bind variables. This can be useful when debugging exactly what is going on. 
The WAIT lines show events where the database had to wait before it could finish its operation. This is very useful if a query is taking a long time but not really doing much (for example, not using CPU).   
|  Text  |  Description  |  
| --- | --- |  
|  nam  |  The name of the Wait event.  |  
|  Ela  |  Elapsed time in hundredths of seconds.   |  
|  P1, p2, p3  |  The parameters specific to the event. Each event has its own set of parameters. For example, the p1 parameter of the enqueue Wait event indicates what kind of lock it is waiting on.   |  
The XCTEND line is a transaction end marker. If rlbk is 1, the transaction was rolled back. If rlbk is 0, the transaction was committed. If rd_only is 1, the transaction was read-only. If rd_only is 0, changes occurred.

##### TKPROF
If you run TKPROF on the .trc file, you get an output file with a lot of the trace file information consolidated in a more readable report with summary data. This is an example TKPROF line: 
tkprof testdb_ora_28969.trc testdb_ora_28969.prf sys=no explain=user/pwd@testdb
TKPROF has a number of options. One of the most useful is to sort the report in order of the most expensive SQL in terms of CPU: 
tkprof testdb_ora_28969.trc testdb_ora_28969.prf sys=no explain=user/pwd@testdb sort=(EXECPU)
This is an example of TKPROF output:
