#### Implementing Custom Application Interfaces

##### Creating Basic Placement Techniques

###### Customizing a Basic Placement Technique
Part of customization is specifying whether the technique is silent or interactive, which is also done in metadata. Many ways to customize an interactive Placement Technique involve manipulating the mouse input before sending it to the [IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper ](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_API_IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper.htm)mouse event methods, MouseClick and MouseMove in particular.   
|  Example Alter the input point:
  * Generate multiple points from the input point before it is sent to the appropriate mouse event method. 
  * If the input point is too close to the last input point, discard the new input point.
  * Use the input point to locate an existing graphic component to be used as a reference point. 
  * Add the input point directly to the geometry object, with a later call to the IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper SetGeometry method to display the completed geometry. 
  * Use a KeyUp event to signal the technique to enter or exit arc placement by calling the IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper StartArc or AbortArc methods. 
  * Instead of using mouse events and mouse points, use a dialog box to collect the data necessary to construct the geometry. 

 |  
| --- |  
For more control over the geometry construction process, override the base class’s implementation of any of the IGTPlacementTechnique2 methods or properties. Use the IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper CreateGeometry, AppendGeometry, and SetGeometry methods. When using these methods, keep in mind that adding points directly to the geometry object itself does not result in updated graphics on the screen. The graphics displayed on the screen are not updated until AppendGeometry or SetGeometry is called. Also, if MouseClick and MouseDblClick methods are not used, then you need to call EndPlacement to notify the placement command that the custom technique has completed geometry construction. 
Here are the various user actions that can occur during interactive digitization and how the basic interactive technique responds to each:   
|  User action  |  Response  |  
| --- | --- |  
|  Mouse move during freehand mode  |  The MouseMove method of the IGTPlacementTechnique is called. It calls MouseMove on IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper, which displays the dynamic geometry in rubber band mode.   |  
|  Mouse move when a construction aid is active  |  The mouse move is given directly to IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper, which displays the dynamic geometry appropriate for the construction aid that is running.   |  
|  Mouse move during common adjustments  |  The mouse move is given directly to IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper, which displays the dynamic geometry for common adjustments. This means the current geometry is put into a move, rotate, or flip mode.   |  
|  Left click during freehand mode  |  The MouseClick method of the IGTPlacementTechnique is called. It calls MouseClick on IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper, which appends the mouse click point to the geometry and displays it. If constructing a point or text point, then a mouse click completes the geometry and either signals that the technique is finished or enters it into common adjustment mode.   |  
|  Left click when a construction aid is active  |  The mouse click is given directly to IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper. It is used by the construction aid to locate an existing geometry or is appended to the geometry the Aid is constructing.   |  
|  Left click during common adjustments  |  MouseClick method is bypassed and the mouse click is given directly to IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper, which it uses to determine a new adjusted location for the geometry.   |  
|  Right-click during freehand  |  If the custom placement technique sets base.RightMouseClickEnabled to true, this action responds the same as Left click during freehand mode, except that the value of the “Button” argument passed to the IGTPlacementTechnique MouseClick is 2.  If the custom placement technique sets base.RightMouseClickEnabled to false, this event is consumed by the placement system and results in the relationship tip dialog being displayed. This dialog shows which relationships can be established at the current mouse location if the user were to click here.   |  
|  Right-click when a construction aid is active  |  This event is consumed by the placement system and results in the relationship tip dialog being displayed. This dialog shows which relationships can be established at the current mouse location if the user were to click here.   |  
|  Right-click during common adjustments  |  MouseClick method is bypassed and the mouse click is given directly to IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper, which uses the right mouse click to skip the current adjustment.   |  
|  Mouse double-click during freehand mode  |  The MouseDblClick method of the IGTPlacementTechnique is called. It calls MouseDblClick on IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper, which completes the geometry and either signal that the technique is finished or enter common adjustment mode.   |  
|  Mouse double-click during a construction aid or common adjustments  |  The mouse double-click is given directly to IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper. Construction aids and common adjustments ignore a double-click.   |  
|  KeyUp for backspace during freehand mode  |  The IGTPlacementTechnique KeyUp method is called. It calls KeyUp on IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper, which removes the last point digitized from the geometry.   |  
|  KeyUp for backspace during a construction aid or common adjustments  |  The KeyUp is given directly to IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper. Construction aids and common adjustments ignore a backspace.   |  
|  KeyUp for F1 during freehand mode  |  KeyUp method is called. The IGTPlacementTechnique may display its own help topic. If KeyUp is called on IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper, it displays an error that it does not provide a help topic.   |  
|  KeyUp for F1 during a construction aid  |  The key up is given directly to IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper, which displays help for the construction aid that is running.   |  
|  KeyUp for F1 during common adjustments  |  The key up is given directly to IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper. Common adjustments ignore F1 key up events.   |  
|  KeyUp for ESC during any mode  |  The AbortPlacement method on and on IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper is called. The result of an ESC is the termination of the placement command with all work against the current feature being discarded.   |  
|  KeyUp for SHIFT- ESC during any mode  |  The AbortPlacement method on IGTPlacementTechnique and on IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper is called. A SHIFT-ESC causes the Placement Technique that is currently running to be terminated. Dynamics displayed for the component being digitized are erased and its geometry is discarded. The command remains running.   |

###### Implementing Silent Placement Techniques
To implement a silent Placement Technique, you must first [implement a basic Placement Technique object](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/B3AyDc9UYsQ_5ndyu_gcwg). 
  * To turn a basic placement technique into a silent technique:


  1. Override the base classes StartPlacement method. Do not call the base class’s StartPlacement method. By not calling the base class’s StartPlacement method, mouse input processing is not initialized. Since this is a silent technique, there is no mouse input to process. 
  2. In StartPlacement, disable Construction Aids and status bar prompts by setting ConstructionAidsEnabled to GTConstructionAidsEnabledConstants.gtptConstructionAids and StatusBarPromptsEnabled to False. 
  3. All of the code to construct the geometry should be located in the StartPlacement method, and by the time this method finishes, the geometry should be complete. 
  4. Add a call to the IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper CreateGeometry method to create a new geometry object. 
  5. Parse the Placement argument array provided in the GraphicComponent property.
  6. Use the geometry for the relative component from the GraphicComponents collection as a reference to construct the geometry for this component. 
  7. Access the new geometry object directly to add the points you want.
  8. Use the IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper SetGeometry method to get it displayed on the screen. 
  9. To signal that the silent technique has completed, call the IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper EndPlacement method.

###### Support Objects for Custom Placement Techniques
NetWorks Core provides four support objects to help you customize the basic Placement Technique object. 
  * IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper
The [IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper object](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_API_IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper.htm) provides access to construction aids and common adjustments, and is primarily used for interactive placement. This object: 
    * Contains mouse-event handling that processes mouse moves and clicks to generate dynamic geometry and vertex points. 
    * Provides events and methods for arc placement.
    * Includes direct access to the geometry object, which lets the user create and manipulate the geometry. This is useful in both silent and interactive techniques. 
    * Provides access to the Construction Aids control, which contains advanced tools for geometry construction. These are useful only to interactive techniques. 
    * Provides Common Adjustment functionality, which lets the geometry be moved or rotated once digitizing is complete. This functionality is also useful in both silent and interactive techniques. 
  * IGTPlacementTechniqueEventMode 
The [IGTPlacementTechniqueEventMode object](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_API_IGTPlacementTechniqueEventMode.htm) controls when the placement system processes relationships. This object contains a property that lets the technique disable relationship processing during mouse events such as mouse moves and clicks. This is useful if a mouse event was consumed for purposes other than geometry construction. Only interactive techniques can take advantage of this object. 
  * IGTGraphicComponent
The [IGTGraphicComponent object](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_API_IGTGraphicComponent.htm) provides key information about digitized components such as the key identity fields, Placement Technique arguments, and component geometry. 
This object is used by both silent and interactive techniques to gain access to the Placement arguments that have been defined for this component. 
  * IGTGraphicComponents
The [IGTGraphicComponents](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_API_IGTGraphicComponents.htm) collection also provides key information about digitized components. 
This object is used primarily by silent techniques to determine which component is the relative component so that its geometry can be accessed for reference purposes. 


These are suggestions for using the support interfaces.
  * Specify which construction aids to use.
  * Control whether the construction aids alter the dynamic display of the geometry on mouse moves. 


Control whether the constructed geometry created by the construction aids is automatically appended to the current geometry. 
  * This involves setting the ConstructionAidComplete event AutomaticallyAppend parameter to False, making the changes to the constructed geometry, and then appending the constructed geometry to the current geometry using the IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper AppendGeometry method. 


![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/259690) A custom placement technique does not receive any mouse events while a construction aid is running, but is notified when the construction aid has finished using the ConstructionAidComplete event. 
  * Control whether the technique performs common adjustments and which adjustments occur by using the Graphic Adjustment argument in the Placement argument array of the IGTGraphicComponent object. 
  * If no Graphic Adjustment argument is defined, common adjustments are not applied. However, if a Graphic Adjustment argument is defined, the IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper uses it to determine what common adjustments to apply to the geometry. 


![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/259690) A custom placement technique does not receive any mouse events while common adjustments are in progress. Once all the specified adjustments have been invoked, the technique is considered to be finished. 
  * Modify a technique to display its own status bar prompts. The IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper supplies status bar prompts by default, but these can be eliminated by setting the StatusBarPromptsEnabled property to False. The technique can then display its own status bar prompts using the StatusBarText method. 
  * There are numerous ways to collect and process input for the geometry construction process. The simplest method for processing the input is to use the IGTPlacementTechniqueHelper mouse event methods. These methods provide dynamic rubber banding with every MouseMove, append vertex points with every MouseClick, and complete the geometry on MouseClick or MouseDblClick, depending on the geometry type.

###### What Not To Include in a Placement Technique
There are certain things you should not try within a custom Placement Technique, as the Placement system does not react appropriately, including the following: 
  * Directly calling the relationship services to perform relationship processing.
  * Broadcasting database changes out to the system.
  * Database transaction processing.
  * Deleting components from the current feature instance.
  * Creating or modifying components on other feature instances that need to be visible or used in relationship to the feature component being created. The system is not able to digitize multiple components at the same time.

##### Designing Temporary Geometry Placement Interfaces

###### Implementing Temporary Geometry Placement Objects
You create Temporary Geometry Placement objects through Metadata Explorer and implement the properties and methods of the [IGTTemporaryGeometryPlacement](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_Interfaces_IGTTemporaryGeometryPlacement.htm) interface. 
![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260605) To perform these steps, you must be connected to a database for which you have administrative privileges. 
To implement an interface using .NET, [click here](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260605). 
This is an overview workflow for implementing a .NET custom extension in NetWorks Core. 
  * To implement a .NET custom extension:


  1. Produce a .NET custom extension type in a .NET custom extension assembly:
     * The .NET custom extension project must add a reference to the Intergraph.GTechnology.dll assembly located in the \GTechnology\Program folder. This assembly is not deployed in the Global Assembly Cache (GAC). The assembly contains the public namespaces Intergraph.CoordinateSystems, Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces, and Intergraph.GTechnology.API. 
     * Inherit a .NET custom extension type from a NetWorks Core public interface defined in the public namespace Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces. The .NET custom extension type can use .NET helper objects from the public namespace Intergraph.GTechnology.API. 
     * The .NET custom extension type should carefully consider the type of work performed and the access to feature data. On occasion, it is necessary to force system Garbage Corrector (GC) to reclaim unused memory. When the NetWorks Core session is terminated, the framework does the required cleaning. As part of the clean-up processing, the framework forces GC to run. However, if you manipulate a large number of ADO recordsets and/or a large number of NetWorks Core features, it is also appropriate to force GC to run in those .NET custom extensions. 
It is also an essential .NET coding practice to call the Dispose method, when available, and when you are done using those .NET objects. For example, call the IGTFeaturePlacementService.Dispose method when you are done using the .NET helper object from your .NET custom extension type. This is the proper garbage collection sequence: 
Call any Dispose methods on objects that you are using;
Release any objects that do not naturally fall out of scope
Call the garbage collection sequence noted here when you have processed a large number of ADO recordsets and/or IGTKeyObject. 
GC.Collect();
GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
GC.Collect();
     * ![Warning](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260605) There are some programming practices that must be followed in custom code: 
       * Only use local variables to store pointers to NetWorks Core windows. Never store them as global variables or even class variables. 
       * Never call methods that refresh the database while there are objects in the select set. These APIs (and maybe more) refresh the database: 
- GTJobManagementService.RefreshJobEnvironment
- GTTransactionManager.RefreshDatabaseChanges
- GTTransactionManager.Commit
- The methods on JobHelper that change the job context
       * Never change the job context when writing functional interfaces, especially validation interfaces. 
  2. Place the .NET custom extension assembly in the \GTechnology\Program folder for testing purposes. 
  3. Using Metadata Explorer, populate the required NetWorks Core interface point metadata to add the .NET custom extension, and refresh or publish metadata. 
    1. In the Metadata Explorer tree view, select the Software Interfaces node and navigate to the appropriate .NET interface, for example, Compute Partial Start Length 
    2. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260605), or right-click and select Insert a new row. 
    3. Populate the new row in the interface table that appears in the Metadata Explorer content panel: 
      1. In the G3E_USERNAME field, type a descriptive name for the object.  
This name appears in the tree view. 
      2. In the G3E_INTERFACE field, type a name for the .NET assembly. The value in the G3E_INTERFACE field must be in the following format:  
AssemblyName:TypeName  
where 
AssemblyName is the filename of the assembly containing the .NET custom extension, and TypeName is the type name (namespace.classname) of the .NET custom extension.   
|  Example GTDotNetSamples:Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample  AssemblyName is GTDotNetSamples. TypeName is Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample with namespace as Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples and classname as GTDisableEditToolSample.  |  
| --- |  
      3. Click OK. 
    4. To update existing arguments for your object:
      1. In the tree view under your new .NET interface, select the Arguments node.
      2. Select the argument you want to update.
      3. Update the fields that are available for edit, and click somewhere else on the screen.
      4. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260605) to commit your edits to the database. 
      5. Repeat these steps for each argument.
    5. To add arguments to your interface:
      1. In the tree view under your new .NET interface, select the Arguments node.
      2. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260605), or right-click and select Insert a new row. 
      3. In the argument table that appears in the Metadata Explorer content panel:
       * Type a number to indicate the order of the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTORDINAL field.
       * Type a name for the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTNAME field.
       * Describe the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTDESCRIPTION field.
       * From the G3E_ARGUMENTTYPE drop-down list, select a data type.
       * Click OK. 
      1. Repeat Steps ii and iii for each argument you want to add.
    6. [Complete configuration](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/2LDawReDio_37hAl4p5itA) of the new interface by associating it with a feature, component, attribute, and so forth so that a user can access it. 
  4. Test the .NET custom extension type by running a NetWorks Core command that exposes the interface point. If you are implementing a custom command, then you would invoke your custom command to test your code. 
  5. Publish and distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension assembly either to a shared location defined in the [FileUNCPaths.xml file](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/vh0Kk8wYIT3X~Tvx5EvjTQ) under the <CUSTOMIZATION> and <DOTNET> tags or distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension to every local client machine. 
On the client machine, the .NET custom extension assembly should be either placed in the \GTechnology\Program folder or deployed into the GAC, so that users can access the assembly at runtime. 
The .NET custom extension assemblies can be deployed into the GAC by using Windows Explorer to drag assemblies into GAC, by using a Windows Installer package you have developed, or by using the developer GAC tool, Gacutil.exe, which is delivered with the .NET framework SDK. 


If a location is defined in FileUNCPaths.xml, and .NET custom extension assemblies exist on both local and remote machines, the local copy takes precedence.

The .NET custom extension assemblies can be deployed into the GAC by using Windows Explorer to drag assemblies into GAC, by using a Windows Installer package you have developed, or by using the developer GAC tool, Gacutil.exe, which is delivered with the .NET framework SDK. 


If a location is defined in FileUNCPaths.xml, and .NET custom extension assemblies exist on both local and remote machines, the local copy takes precedence.

##### Implementing Custom Plot Objects
You create Custom Plot objects through Metadata Explorer and implement the properties and methods of the [IGTCustomPlot](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_Interfaces_IGTCustomPlot.htm) interface. You modify the IGTCustomPlot_InitializePlot and IGTCustomPlot_PlotPrepared methods in the template to achieve the appropriate workflow. 
![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/258422) To perform these steps, you must be connected to a database for which you have administrative privileges. 
To implement an interface using .NET, [click here](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/258422). 
This is an overview workflow for implementing a .NET custom extension in NetWorks Core. 
  * To implement a .NET custom extension:


  1. Produce a .NET custom extension type in a .NET custom extension assembly:
     * The .NET custom extension project must add a reference to the Intergraph.GTechnology.dll assembly located in the \GTechnology\Program folder. This assembly is not deployed in the Global Assembly Cache (GAC). The assembly contains the public namespaces Intergraph.CoordinateSystems, Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces, and Intergraph.GTechnology.API. 
     * Inherit a .NET custom extension type from a NetWorks Core public interface defined in the public namespace Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces. The .NET custom extension type can use .NET helper objects from the public namespace Intergraph.GTechnology.API. 
     * The .NET custom extension type should carefully consider the type of work performed and the access to feature data. On occasion, it is necessary to force system Garbage Corrector (GC) to reclaim unused memory. When the NetWorks Core session is terminated, the framework does the required cleaning. As part of the clean-up processing, the framework forces GC to run. However, if you manipulate a large number of ADO recordsets and/or a large number of NetWorks Core features, it is also appropriate to force GC to run in those .NET custom extensions. 
It is also an essential .NET coding practice to call the Dispose method, when available, and when you are done using those .NET objects. For example, call the IGTFeaturePlacementService.Dispose method when you are done using the .NET helper object from your .NET custom extension type. This is the proper garbage collection sequence: 
Call any Dispose methods on objects that you are using;
Release any objects that do not naturally fall out of scope
Call the garbage collection sequence noted here when you have processed a large number of ADO recordsets and/or IGTKeyObject. 
GC.Collect();
GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
GC.Collect();
     * ![Warning](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/258422) There are some programming practices that must be followed in custom code: 
       * Only use local variables to store pointers to NetWorks Core windows. Never store them as global variables or even class variables. 
       * Never call methods that refresh the database while there are objects in the select set. These APIs (and maybe more) refresh the database: 
- GTJobManagementService.RefreshJobEnvironment
- GTTransactionManager.RefreshDatabaseChanges
- GTTransactionManager.Commit
- The methods on JobHelper that change the job context
       * Never change the job context when writing functional interfaces, especially validation interfaces. 
  2. Place the .NET custom extension assembly in the \GTechnology\Program folder for testing purposes. 
  3. Using Metadata Explorer, populate the required NetWorks Core interface point metadata to add the .NET custom extension, and refresh or publish metadata. 
    1. In the Metadata Explorer tree view, select the Software Interfaces node and navigate to the appropriate .NET interface, for example, Compute Partial Start Length 
    2. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/258422), or right-click and select Insert a new row. 
    3. Populate the new row in the interface table that appears in the Metadata Explorer content panel: 
      1. In the G3E_USERNAME field, type a descriptive name for the object.  
This name appears in the tree view. 
      2. In the G3E_INTERFACE field, type a name for the .NET assembly. The value in the G3E_INTERFACE field must be in the following format:  
AssemblyName:TypeName  
where 
AssemblyName is the filename of the assembly containing the .NET custom extension, and TypeName is the type name (namespace.classname) of the .NET custom extension.   
|  Example GTDotNetSamples:Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample  AssemblyName is GTDotNetSamples. TypeName is Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample with namespace as Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples and classname as GTDisableEditToolSample.  |  
| --- |  
      3. Click OK. 
    4. To update existing arguments for your object:
      1. In the tree view under your new .NET interface, select the Arguments node.
      2. Select the argument you want to update.
      3. Update the fields that are available for edit, and click somewhere else on the screen.
      4. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/258422) to commit your edits to the database. 
      5. Repeat these steps for each argument.
    5. To add arguments to your interface:
      1. In the tree view under your new .NET interface, select the Arguments node.
      2. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/258422), or right-click and select Insert a new row. 
      3. In the argument table that appears in the Metadata Explorer content panel:
       * Type a number to indicate the order of the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTORDINAL field.
       * Type a name for the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTNAME field.
       * Describe the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTDESCRIPTION field.
       * From the G3E_ARGUMENTTYPE drop-down list, select a data type.
       * Click OK. 
      1. Repeat Steps ii and iii for each argument you want to add.
    6. [Complete configuration](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/2LDawReDio_37hAl4p5itA) of the new interface by associating it with a feature, component, attribute, and so forth so that a user can access it. 
  4. Test the .NET custom extension type by running a NetWorks Core command that exposes the interface point. If you are implementing a custom command, then you would invoke your custom command to test your code. 
  5. Publish and distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension assembly either to a shared location defined in the [FileUNCPaths.xml file](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/vh0Kk8wYIT3X~Tvx5EvjTQ) under the <CUSTOMIZATION> and <DOTNET> tags or distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension to every local client machine. 
On the client machine, the .NET custom extension assembly should be either placed in the \GTechnology\Program folder or deployed into the GAC, so that users can access the assembly at runtime. 
The .NET custom extension assemblies can be deployed into the GAC by using Windows Explorer to drag assemblies into GAC, by using a Windows Installer package you have developed, or by using the developer GAC tool, Gacutil.exe, which is delivered with the .NET framework SDK. 


If a location is defined in FileUNCPaths.xml, and .NET custom extension assemblies exist on both local and remote machines, the local copy takes precedence.

Publish and distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension assembly either to a shared location defined in the [FileUNCPaths.xml file](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/vh0Kk8wYIT3X~Tvx5EvjTQ) under the <CUSTOMIZATION> and <DOTNET> tags or distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension to every local client machine. 
On the client machine, the .NET custom extension assembly should be either placed in the \GTechnology\Program folder or deployed into the GAC, so that users can access the assembly at runtime. 
The .NET custom extension assemblies can be deployed into the GAC by using Windows Explorer to drag assemblies into GAC, by using a Windows Installer package you have developed, or by using the developer GAC tool, Gacutil.exe, which is delivered with the .NET framework SDK. 


If a location is defined in FileUNCPaths.xml, and .NET custom extension assemblies exist on both local and remote machines, the local copy takes precedence.

##### Implementing Foreign Key Query Objects
You create Foreign Key Query objects through Metadata Explorer and implement the properties and methods of the [IGTForeignKeyQuery](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_Interfaces_IGTForeignKeyQuery.htm) interface. Finally, you must configure and then publish metadata. 
![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260554) To perform these steps, you must be connected to a database for which you have administrative privileges. 
To implement an interface using .NET, [click here](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260554). 
This is an overview workflow for implementing a .NET custom extension in NetWorks Core. 
  * To implement a .NET custom extension:


  1. Produce a .NET custom extension type in a .NET custom extension assembly:
     * The .NET custom extension project must add a reference to the Intergraph.GTechnology.dll assembly located in the \GTechnology\Program folder. This assembly is not deployed in the Global Assembly Cache (GAC). The assembly contains the public namespaces Intergraph.CoordinateSystems, Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces, and Intergraph.GTechnology.API. 
     * Inherit a .NET custom extension type from a NetWorks Core public interface defined in the public namespace Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces. The .NET custom extension type can use .NET helper objects from the public namespace Intergraph.GTechnology.API. 
     * The .NET custom extension type should carefully consider the type of work performed and the access to feature data. On occasion, it is necessary to force system Garbage Corrector (GC) to reclaim unused memory. When the NetWorks Core session is terminated, the framework does the required cleaning. As part of the clean-up processing, the framework forces GC to run. However, if you manipulate a large number of ADO recordsets and/or a large number of NetWorks Core features, it is also appropriate to force GC to run in those .NET custom extensions. 
It is also an essential .NET coding practice to call the Dispose method, when available, and when you are done using those .NET objects. For example, call the IGTFeaturePlacementService.Dispose method when you are done using the .NET helper object from your .NET custom extension type. This is the proper garbage collection sequence: 
Call any Dispose methods on objects that you are using;
Release any objects that do not naturally fall out of scope
Call the garbage collection sequence noted here when you have processed a large number of ADO recordsets and/or IGTKeyObject. 
GC.Collect();
GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
GC.Collect();
     * ![Warning](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260554) There are some programming practices that must be followed in custom code: 
       * Only use local variables to store pointers to NetWorks Core windows. Never store them as global variables or even class variables. 
       * Never call methods that refresh the database while there are objects in the select set. These APIs (and maybe more) refresh the database: 
- GTJobManagementService.RefreshJobEnvironment
- GTTransactionManager.RefreshDatabaseChanges
- GTTransactionManager.Commit
- The methods on JobHelper that change the job context
       * Never change the job context when writing functional interfaces, especially validation interfaces. 
  2. Place the .NET custom extension assembly in the \GTechnology\Program folder for testing purposes. 
  3. Using Metadata Explorer, populate the required NetWorks Core interface point metadata to add the .NET custom extension, and refresh or publish metadata. 
    1. In the Metadata Explorer tree view, select the Software Interfaces node and navigate to the appropriate .NET interface, for example, Compute Partial Start Length 
    2. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260554), or right-click and select Insert a new row. 
    3. Populate the new row in the interface table that appears in the Metadata Explorer content panel: 
      1. In the G3E_USERNAME field, type a descriptive name for the object.  
This name appears in the tree view. 
      2. In the G3E_INTERFACE field, type a name for the .NET assembly. The value in the G3E_INTERFACE field must be in the following format:  
AssemblyName:TypeName  
where 
AssemblyName is the filename of the assembly containing the .NET custom extension, and TypeName is the type name (namespace.classname) of the .NET custom extension.   
|  Example GTDotNetSamples:Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample  AssemblyName is GTDotNetSamples. TypeName is Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample with namespace as Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples and classname as GTDisableEditToolSample.  |  
| --- |  
      3. Click OK. 
    4. To update existing arguments for your object:
      1. In the tree view under your new .NET interface, select the Arguments node.
      2. Select the argument you want to update.
      3. Update the fields that are available for edit, and click somewhere else on the screen.
      4. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260554) to commit your edits to the database. 
      5. Repeat these steps for each argument.
    5. To add arguments to your interface:
      1. In the tree view under your new .NET interface, select the Arguments node.
      2. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260554), or right-click and select Insert a new row. 
      3. In the argument table that appears in the Metadata Explorer content panel:
       * Type a number to indicate the order of the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTORDINAL field.
       * Type a name for the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTNAME field.
       * Describe the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTDESCRIPTION field.
       * From the G3E_ARGUMENTTYPE drop-down list, select a data type.
       * Click OK. 
      1. Repeat Steps ii and iii for each argument you want to add.
    6. [Complete configuration](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/2LDawReDio_37hAl4p5itA) of the new interface by associating it with a feature, component, attribute, and so forth so that a user can access it. 
  4. Test the .NET custom extension type by running a NetWorks Core command that exposes the interface point. If you are implementing a custom command, then you would invoke your custom command to test your code. 
  5. Publish and distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension assembly either to a shared location defined in the [FileUNCPaths.xml file](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/vh0Kk8wYIT3X~Tvx5EvjTQ) under the <CUSTOMIZATION> and <DOTNET> tags or distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension to every local client machine. 
On the client machine, the .NET custom extension assembly should be either placed in the \GTechnology\Program folder or deployed into the GAC, so that users can access the assembly at runtime. 
The .NET custom extension assemblies can be deployed into the GAC by using Windows Explorer to drag assemblies into GAC, by using a Windows Installer package you have developed, or by using the developer GAC tool, Gacutil.exe, which is delivered with the .NET framework SDK. 


If a location is defined in FileUNCPaths.xml, and .NET custom extension assemblies exist on both local and remote machines, the local copy takes precedence.

##### Implementing Functional Objects
You create Functional objects through Metadata Explorer and implement the properties and methods of the IGTFunctional interface. 
The Functional object must be associated with an attribute of a component. Because component views are not edited, you cannot associate a Functional object to a component view. For similar reasons, you cannot associate a Functional object to a special component (G3E_TYPE = 2048).

##### Implementing Import Feature Objects
You create Import Feature objects through Metadata Explorer and implement the properties and methods of the [IGTImportFeature](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_Interfaces_IGTImportFeature.htm) interface. 
The Execute method should include the code to read the input data source file and to create new or update existing feature attribute information. Once the feature information is collected from the input file, it can perform feature manipulation and maintain database transactions in one of two ways: 
  * Using the DataContext property to create or edit features and the TransactionManager property to maintain the database transactions. 
  * Using the input parameter IGTFeatureLoaderService.


The IGTFeatureLoaderService is an input parameter provided only to support existing workflows that are already implemented. If you are implementing a new Import Feature object and do not need the ability to establish a relationship or break a linear feature, use the DataContext and TransactionManager properties to create or edit features and to maintain the database transactions.   
|  ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260558) The interface must use one approach exclusively. That is, you cannot use GTFeatureLoader.BeginTrans and IGTTransactionManager.Commit, as this results in errors and inconsistent results.   |  
| --- |

       * Describe the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTDESCRIPTION field.
       * From the G3E_ARGUMENTTYPE drop-down list, select a data type.
       * Click OK. 
      1. Repeat Steps ii and iii for each argument you want to add.
    6. [Complete configuration](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/2LDawReDio_37hAl4p5itA) of the new interface by associating it with a feature, component, attribute, and so forth so that a user can access it. 
  4. Test the .NET custom extension type by running a NetWorks Core command that exposes the interface point. If you are implementing a custom command, then you would invoke your custom command to test your code. 
  5. Publish and distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension assembly either to a shared location defined in the [FileUNCPaths.xml file](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/vh0Kk8wYIT3X~Tvx5EvjTQ) under the <CUSTOMIZATION> and <DOTNET> tags or distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension to every local client machine. 
On the client machine, the .NET custom extension assembly should be either placed in the \GTechnology\Program folder or deployed into the GAC, so that users can access the assembly at runtime. 
The .NET custom extension assemblies can be deployed into the GAC by using Windows Explorer to drag assemblies into GAC, by using a Windows Installer package you have developed, or by using the developer GAC tool, Gacutil.exe, which is delivered with the .NET framework SDK. 


If a location is defined in FileUNCPaths.xml, and .NET custom extension assemblies exist on both local and remote machines, the local copy takes precedence.

##### Implementing Merge Features Objects
You create Merge Features objects through Metadata Explorer and implement the properties and methods of the [IGTMergeFeatures](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_Interfaces_IGTMergeFeatures.htm) interface. 
Next you add code to the Allow and Approve methods with any custom checking to see if the two features are valid to be merged. As the Allow method is called before any user interaction, the maximum amount of checking should be done here. The MergeComponents method should be implemented if any custom merging of the geometries is necessary. Any post process actions should be added to the PostProcess method. Methods that do no processing should always return True. 
After the metadata is published and refreshed, the interface is invoked the next time the feature with which it is associated is merged. 
![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260571) To perform these steps, you must be connected to a database for which you have administrative privileges. 
To implement an interface using .NET, [click here](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260571). 
This is an overview workflow for implementing a .NET custom extension in NetWorks Core. 
  * To implement a .NET custom extension:


  1. Produce a .NET custom extension type in a .NET custom extension assembly:
     * The .NET custom extension project must add a reference to the Intergraph.GTechnology.dll assembly located in the \GTechnology\Program folder. This assembly is not deployed in the Global Assembly Cache (GAC). The assembly contains the public namespaces Intergraph.CoordinateSystems, Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces, and Intergraph.GTechnology.API. 
     * Inherit a .NET custom extension type from a NetWorks Core public interface defined in the public namespace Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces. The .NET custom extension type can use .NET helper objects from the public namespace Intergraph.GTechnology.API. 
     * The .NET custom extension type should carefully consider the type of work performed and the access to feature data. On occasion, it is necessary to force system Garbage Corrector (GC) to reclaim unused memory. When the NetWorks Core session is terminated, the framework does the required cleaning. As part of the clean-up processing, the framework forces GC to run. However, if you manipulate a large number of ADO recordsets and/or a large number of NetWorks Core features, it is also appropriate to force GC to run in those .NET custom extensions. 
It is also an essential .NET coding practice to call the Dispose method, when available, and when you are done using those .NET objects. For example, call the IGTFeaturePlacementService.Dispose method when you are done using the .NET helper object from your .NET custom extension type. This is the proper garbage collection sequence: 
Call any Dispose methods on objects that you are using;
Release any objects that do not naturally fall out of scope
Call the garbage collection sequence noted here when you have processed a large number of ADO recordsets and/or IGTKeyObject. 
GC.Collect();
GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
GC.Collect();
     * ![Warning](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260571) There are some programming practices that must be followed in custom code: 
       * Only use local variables to store pointers to NetWorks Core windows. Never store them as global variables or even class variables. 
       * Never call methods that refresh the database while there are objects in the select set. These APIs (and maybe more) refresh the database: 
- GTJobManagementService.RefreshJobEnvironment
- GTTransactionManager.RefreshDatabaseChanges
- GTTransactionManager.Commit
- The methods on JobHelper that change the job context
       * Never change the job context when writing functional interfaces, especially validation interfaces. 
  2. Place the .NET custom extension assembly in the \GTechnology\Program folder for testing purposes. 
  3. Using Metadata Explorer, populate the required NetWorks Core interface point metadata to add the .NET custom extension, and refresh or publish metadata. 
    1. In the Metadata Explorer tree view, select the Software Interfaces node and navigate to the appropriate .NET interface, for example, Compute Partial Start Length 
    2. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260571), or right-click and select Insert a new row. 
    3. Populate the new row in the interface table that appears in the Metadata Explorer content panel: 
      1. In the G3E_USERNAME field, type a descriptive name for the object.  
This name appears in the tree view. 
      2. In the G3E_INTERFACE field, type a name for the .NET assembly. The value in the G3E_INTERFACE field must be in the following format:  
AssemblyName:TypeName  
where 
AssemblyName is the filename of the assembly containing the .NET custom extension, and TypeName is the type name (namespace.classname) of the .NET custom extension.   
|  Example GTDotNetSamples:Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample  AssemblyName is GTDotNetSamples. TypeName is Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample with namespace as Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples and classname as GTDisableEditToolSample.  |  
| --- |  
      3. Click OK. 
    4. To update existing arguments for your object:
      1. In the tree view under your new .NET interface, select the Arguments node.
      2. Select the argument you want to update.
      3. Update the fields that are available for edit, and click somewhere else on the screen.
      4. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260571) to commit your edits to the database. 
      5. Repeat these steps for each argument.
    5. To add arguments to your interface:

       * Describe the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTDESCRIPTION field.
       * From the G3E_ARGUMENTTYPE drop-down list, select a data type.
       * Click OK. 
      1. Repeat Steps ii and iii for each argument you want to add.
    6. [Complete configuration](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/2LDawReDio_37hAl4p5itA) of the new interface by associating it with a feature, component, attribute, and so forth so that a user can access it.

##### Implementing Post Break Linear Objects
Post Break objects are defined in the G3E_RELATIONINTERFACE table. To use them, you make entries in the G3E_POSTBREAKMAPPING table to associate a linear graphic component that can be the subject of a break operation to a Post Break object. The G3E_ORDINAL column in this table specifies the order in which the Post Break objects are applied if more than one is associated with the same component. 
You create Post Break Linear objects through Metadata Explorer and implement the properties and methods of the [IGTPostBreakLinear](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_Interfaces_IGTPostBreakLinear.htm) interface. The Execute method should include the code to update the attribution or geometries in question based on the BreakFeature and NewFeature IGTKeyObjects. These IGTKeyObjects and metadata can be read from to make decisions on how to update specific attributes and geometries within these features. All changes made to these objects are updated in the database by the Break subsystem. 
After the metadata is published, the object is invoked the next time the component with which it is associated is involved in a break operation.

##### Implementing Post Process Objects
For .NET, a Post Process object is a .NET class that implements the Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces.IGTPostProcess interface. 
Post Process objects are defined in the G3E_POSTPROCESSINTERFACE table through Metadata Explorer, which contains the list of functions available as Post Processing objects. Each function is effectively an automated object that supports the Post Processing object definition. It is called to support modifications of features based on trace analysis. The specific uses of the Post Process objects are defined in the G3E_POSTPROCESS table. 
The G3E_POSTMAPPING table defines the post processing that can be used by specific queries. This is necessary to prevent query or trace results from being sent to a post process that cannot process them or to prevent incorrect trace contents from being used as input to the post process. While the metadata is defined to allow any query to be used as input, the user interface exposes only trace results to post processing.

  3. Using Metadata Explorer, populate the required NetWorks Core interface point metadata to add the .NET custom extension, and refresh or publish metadata. 
    1. In the Metadata Explorer tree view, select the Software Interfaces node and navigate to the appropriate .NET interface, for example, Compute Partial Start Length 
    2. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260524), or right-click and select Insert a new row. 
    3. Populate the new row in the interface table that appears in the Metadata Explorer content panel: 
      1. In the G3E_USERNAME field, type a descriptive name for the object.  
This name appears in the tree view. 
      2. In the G3E_INTERFACE field, type a name for the .NET assembly. The value in the G3E_INTERFACE field must be in the following format:  
AssemblyName:TypeName  
where 
AssemblyName is the filename of the assembly containing the .NET custom extension, and TypeName is the type name (namespace.classname) of the .NET custom extension.   
|  Example GTDotNetSamples:Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample  AssemblyName is GTDotNetSamples. TypeName is Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample with namespace as Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples and classname as GTDisableEditToolSample.  |  
| --- |  
      3. Click OK. 
    4. To update existing arguments for your object:
      1. In the tree view under your new .NET interface, select the Arguments node.
      2. Select the argument you want to update.
      3. Update the fields that are available for edit, and click somewhere else on the screen.
      4. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260524) to commit your edits to the database. 
      5. Repeat these steps for each argument.
    5. To add arguments to your interface:
      1. In the tree view under your new .NET interface, select the Arguments node.
      2. Click ![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260524), or right-click and select Insert a new row. 
      3. In the argument table that appears in the Metadata Explorer content panel:
       * Type a number to indicate the order of the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTORDINAL field.
       * Type a name for the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTNAME field.
       * Describe the argument in the G3E_ARGUMENTDESCRIPTION field.
       * From the G3E_ARGUMENTTYPE drop-down list, select a data type.
       * Click OK. 
      1. Repeat Steps ii and iii for each argument you want to add.
    6. [Complete configuration](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/2LDawReDio_37hAl4p5itA) of the new interface by associating it with a feature, component, attribute, and so forth so that a user can access it. 
  4. Test the .NET custom extension type by running a NetWorks Core command that exposes the interface point. If you are implementing a custom command, then you would invoke your custom command to test your code. 
  5. Publish and distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension assembly either to a shared location defined in the [FileUNCPaths.xml file](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/_OIjXZnxNqnWnqZEcXwqLA/vh0Kk8wYIT3X~Tvx5EvjTQ) under the <CUSTOMIZATION> and <DOTNET> tags or distribute the metadata and .NET custom extension to every local client machine. 
On the client machine, the .NET custom extension assembly should be either placed in the \GTechnology\Program folder or deployed into the GAC, so that users can access the assembly at runtime. 
The .NET custom extension assemblies can be deployed into the GAC by using Windows Explorer to drag assemblies into GAC, by using a Windows Installer package you have developed, or by using the developer GAC tool, Gacutil.exe, which is delivered with the .NET framework SDK. 


If a location is defined in FileUNCPaths.xml, and .NET custom extension assemblies exist on both local and remote machines, the local copy takes precedence.

##### Implementing Redline Group Objects

###### RedlineGroupInfoRS
Applies To
GetRedlineGroupInfo Method
Description
RedlineGroupInfoRS is the recordset returned from the IGTRedlineGroup interface. This in-memory recordset is populated in the interface. It contains the necessary information for building one or more redline elements for the Redline Group. Because this recordset exists in memory, no database transaction is involved. 
This recordset has the following fields:
  * GROUP_NO (adInteger)
Redline Group number. In case of multiple groups, this number determines the placement sequence of the groups. The FirstGroupNumber input to GetRedlineGroupInfo method determines the first group to be placed. 
  * USER_PLACE (adSmallInt)
Determines if the Redline Group prompts the user for a placement point (value other than zero), or if the redline group is placed at coordinates saved in X, Y, and Z (zero value). 
  * DATA_TYPE (adBSTR)
The type of redline element. The values are GTRedlineGroupDataTypeConstants.
  * STYLE_NUMBER (adInteger)
Style number to be used for the redline element.
  * ROTATION (adDouble)
Angle of the redline element (not used for line redline elements).
  * X, Y, Z (adVariant)
Arrays with each element containing the components of a coordinate of a redline element relative to the redline group origin. For area geometry, the array elements represent the vertices of the area. 
![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/262539) All coordinates are plot sheet coordinates. The plot sheet coordinate system has its origin at the top-left corner of the paper, with X-coordinates increasing to the right and Y-coordinates increasing downward. Each unit in the coordinate system represents 1/100 of a millimeter; that is, 100 units equals 1 millimeter. 
  * GEOMETRY (adVariant)
Contains the geometry of the redline elements. Plotting software uses the geometry if it is available. Otherwise, plotting software builds the geometry using the information contained in the recordset. The allowed geometry types are 
    * IGTPolylineGeometry
    * IGTCompositePolylineGeometry
    * IGTPolygonGeometry
    * IGTCompositePolygonGeometry
    * IGTOrientedPointGeometry
    * IGTTextPointGeometry
  * TEXT_ALIGNMENT (adInteger)
Number that determines the text alignment.
  * TEXT (adBSTR)
Text string of the text.
  * AREA_HEIGHT (adDouble)
Number that determines the height of the rectangle.
  * AREA_WIDTH (adDouble)
Number that determines the width of the rectangle.


If the GEOMETRY field is null and the following attributes for each geometry type are populated (non-null), the plotting software builds the geometry: 
  * IGTPolylineGeometry and IGTPolygonGeometry
X,Y and Z must be populated, and each attribute is an array. Each element in the array represents a coordinate. 
  * IGTOrientedPointGeometry
X,Y and Z representing the location of the geometry must be populated.
  * IGTTextPointGeometry
X,Y and Z representing the location of the geometry must be populated. The TEXT_ALIGNMENT and TEXT attributes must be populated as well. 


If the GEOMETRY field is non-null and the attributes for that geometry are also non-null, then the software raisea an error. 
When building area geometry based on the user-supplied attributes, the plotting command creates a rectangle with <X,Y,Z> at the upper-left corner. The AREA_HEIGHT and AREA_WIDTH determine the lower-right corner of the rectangle.

##### Implementing Relationship Attribute Objects
You create Relationship Attribute objects and associate them with features through Metadata Explorer. Then you implement the properties and either the AfterEstablish method or the Validate method of the [IGTRelationshipAttribute](Ms-its:Intergraph.GTechnology.Desktop.API.Reference.chm::/html/T_Intergraph_GTechnology_Interfaces_IGTRelationshipAttribute.htm) interface. 
The AfterEstablish method does whatever processing is required immediately following the establishment of a relationship, such as copying attribution from one component to another. The Validate method validates the relationship between the active and the related components. 
![](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260602) To perform these steps, you must be connected to a database for which you have administrative privileges. 
To implement an interface using .NET, [click here](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260602). 
This is an overview workflow for implementing a .NET custom extension in NetWorks Core. 
  * To implement a .NET custom extension:


  1. Produce a .NET custom extension type in a .NET custom extension assembly:
     * The .NET custom extension project must add a reference to the Intergraph.GTechnology.dll assembly located in the \GTechnology\Program folder. This assembly is not deployed in the Global Assembly Cache (GAC). The assembly contains the public namespaces Intergraph.CoordinateSystems, Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces, and Intergraph.GTechnology.API. 
     * Inherit a .NET custom extension type from a NetWorks Core public interface defined in the public namespace Intergraph.GTechnology.Interfaces. The .NET custom extension type can use .NET helper objects from the public namespace Intergraph.GTechnology.API. 
     * The .NET custom extension type should carefully consider the type of work performed and the access to feature data. On occasion, it is necessary to force system Garbage Corrector (GC) to reclaim unused memory. When the NetWorks Core session is terminated, the framework does the required cleaning. As part of the clean-up processing, the framework forces GC to run. However, if you manipulate a large number of ADO recordsets and/or a large number of NetWorks Core features, it is also appropriate to force GC to run in those .NET custom extensions. 
It is also an essential .NET coding practice to call the Dispose method, when available, and when you are done using those .NET objects. For example, call the IGTFeaturePlacementService.Dispose method when you are done using the .NET helper object from your .NET custom extension type. This is the proper garbage collection sequence: 
Call any Dispose methods on objects that you are using;
Release any objects that do not naturally fall out of scope
Call the garbage collection sequence noted here when you have processed a large number of ADO recordsets and/or IGTKeyObject. 
GC.Collect();
GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
GC.Collect();
     * ![Warning](https://hexagonppm.fluidtopics.net/r/en-US/HxGN-NetWorks-Core-Admin-Help/260602) There are some programming practices that must be followed in custom code: 
       * Only use local variables to store pointers to NetWorks Core windows. Never store them as global variables or even class variables. 
       * Never call methods that refresh the database while there are objects in the select set. These APIs (and maybe more) refresh the database: 
- GTJobManagementService.RefreshJobEnvironment
- GTTransactionManager.RefreshDatabaseChanges
- GTTransactionManager.Commit
- The methods on JobHelper that change the job context
       * Never change the job context when writing functional interfaces, especially validation interfaces. 
  2. Place the .NET custom extension assembly in the \GTechnology\Program folder for testing purposes. 
  3. Using Metadata Explorer, populate the required NetWorks Core interface point metadata to add the .NET custom extension, and refresh or publish metadata.

    3. Populate the new row in the interface table that appears in the Metadata Explorer content panel: 
      1. In the G3E_USERNAME field, type a descriptive name for the object.  
This name appears in the tree view. 
      2. In the G3E_INTERFACE field, type a name for the .NET assembly. The value in the G3E_INTERFACE field must be in the following format:  
AssemblyName:TypeName  
where 
AssemblyName is the filename of the assembly containing the .NET custom extension, and TypeName is the type name (namespace.classname) of the .NET custom extension.   
|  Example GTDotNetSamples:Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample  AssemblyName is GTDotNetSamples. TypeName is Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples.GTDisableEditToolSample with namespace as Intergraph.GTechnology.DotNetSamples and classname as GTDisableEditToolSample.  |  
| --- |  
      3. Click OK. 
    4. To update existing arguments for your object:

      2. Select the argument you want to update.
      3. Update the fields that are available for edit, and click somewhere else on the screen.
